title: Alex Marquez withdraws from Qatar GP for surgery
raw_summary: Gresini Ducati rider Alex Marquez will undergo surgery and skip MotoGP's Qatar Grand Prix. While tensions continue to simmer in the paddock over whether or not the series can really go to Qatar next weekend amid the USA/Israel-Iran war, Marquez will in any case be absent from the Lusail round should it go ahead.

article_paragraphs: Gresini Ducati rider Alex Marquez will undergo surgery and skip MotoGP's Qatar Grand Prix.

While tensions continue to simmer in the paddock over whether or not the series can really go to Qatar next weekend amid the USA/Israel-Iran war, Marquez will in any case be absent from the Lusail round should it go ahead.

Though he finished on the podium this Sunday at Sepang, one of his best tracks in MotoGP, Marquez has felt limited by continued management of a right shoulder injury he sustained in his brutal crash during the Catalan Grand Prix in May.
"From the moment that I came back after the Catalunya accident, I suffered a lot with my right shoulder," he said.
"I decided tomorrow to take a surgery in Madrid. I will try to come back in Portimao [in three weeks' time]."
The operation, which Marquez described as "two surgeries in one", will remove a big plate from his shoulder but also drain liquid and try to reduce inflammation.
As it stands, Marquez has been unable to do any fitness work at home in this part of the season, saying: "I don't have muscle, I don't have nothing."
He has been racing with the help of injections, but indicated these were proving increasingly ineffective, especially with races on consecutive weekends.

article_paragraphs: Honda has spent decades building one of the most dominant positions in the global motorcycle industry, selling millions of gasoline-powered two-wheelers each year. But in markets where electric motorcycles and scooters are becoming increasingly accessible, that dominance is starting to face a serious challenge.
Vietnam offers a particularly interesting case study, where rapidly growing electric motorcycle sales are beginning to reshape a market long dominated by Honda.

According to newly released nationwide sales figures , Vietnam saw more than 3 million motorcycle and scooter sales during the first nine months of 2026, representing 25.9% growth over the same period last year.

But the real story is in the electric segment, where sales surged 90.5% to reach 973,247 units. That means electric two-wheelers now account for approximately 32% of all new motorcycle and scooter sales in the country.
And the biggest beneficiary isn’t Honda. It’s actually Vietnamese electric vehicle manufacturer VinFast.

While Honda remains Vietnam’s largest motorcycle manufacturer overall, with sales growing 8.4% this year, VinFast has surged into second place with a staggering 152.1% increase in sales. Yamaha now sits in third place, followed by electric two-wheeler manufacturer Yadea in fourth.
Of the top four players, half are electric, and it’s precisely that half that is experiencing meteoric sales growth.
It’s an impressive reshuffling of a market that has traditionally been dominated by Japanese gasoline motorcycle manufacturers.

title: Marquez takes complete control of title fight with Sepang win
raw_summary: Defending MotoGP champion Marc Marquez dominated the Malaysian Grand Prix at Sepang to put one hand on the 2026 title. With main title rival Jorge Martin absent after aborting an attempt to complete the weekend with a broken wrist, Marquez maximised the points damage by winning a race that was lively to begin with but quickly settled into a procession.

With main title rival Jorge Martin absent after aborting an attempt to complete the weekend with a broken wrist, Marquez maximised the points damage by winning a race that was lively to begin with but quickly settled into a procession.
article_paragraphs: Defending MotoGP champion Marc Marquez dominated the Malaysian Grand Prix at Sepang to put one hand on the 2026 title.

With main title rival Jorge Martin absent after aborting an attempt to complete the weekend with a broken wrist, Marquez maximised the points damage by winning a race that was lively to begin with but quickly settled into a procession.
Marquez overtook polesitting brother Alex into Turn 1, then rebuffed a counter-attack at Turn 4 as Alex couldn't quite get his Gresini Ducati stopped to complete the move.

They ran in tandem for the next few laps, with a charging Pedro Acosta moving up to third after a feisty opening lap - but Alex simply had no answer for Marc's pace further into the race, as the gap between the two tipped over a second on lap seven of 20.
By the time Acosta worked his way past Alex Marquez with a move into the hard braking zone of Turn 9, Marc was already nearly two seconds clear.
And the change in second place made little difference to his race, as the elder Marquez ultimately won by a commanding 4.1s - the third-highest grand prix winning margin of the season.
With Acosta and Alex Marquez joining him on the podium, there was further disillusionment for Aprilia late on as Marco Bezzecchi's grand prix fell apart.

Bezzecchi had overtaken Aprilia stablemate Ai Ogura early on, and looked like joining the podium battle - but never quite did, instead falling into the clutches of the Japanese rider in the closing laps.

title: Australian Icon: A 1963 Holden EH “Special”
raw_summary: This is a 1963 Holden EH Special, it’s an Australian sedan that dominated the southern nation’s sales charts back in the 1960s, and remained a common sight on roads until well into the 1980s. This car is an EH Special, denoting the fact that it was a more upmarket version of the model, a special-equipment example with more chrome and better trim. This car had the largest engine on offer, the 179 cubic inch (2.9 liter) straight-six affectionately known as the Holden Red motor.

This car is an EH Special, denoting the fact that it was a more upmarket version of the model, a special-equipment example with more chrome and better trim.
article_paragraphs: This is a 1963 Holden EH Special, it’s an Australian sedan that dominated the southern nation’s sales charts back in the 1960s, and remained a common sight on roads until well into the 1980s.

This car is an EH Special, denoting the fact that it was a more upmarket version of the model, a special-equipment example with more chrome and better trim. This car had the largest engine on offer, the 179 cubic inch (2.9 liter) straight-six affectionately known as the Holden Red motor.

Holden released their new EH model in August of 1963, they would ultimately sell over a quarter of a million of them over three model years, 256,959 in total , and it soon became one of the most common family cars on Australian roads. The body of the EH was closely based on the earlier Holden EJ model, and Holden later described the EH as the fastest-selling Australian car ever.

Holden released their new EH model in August of 1963, they would ultimately sell over a quarter of a million of them over three model years, 256,959 in total, and it soon became one of the most common family cars on Australian roads. Image courtesy of General Motors Holden.

The Holden EJ sedan of mid-1962 had been the first all-new Holden of the decade, it was lower and sleeker than the outgoing EK it replaced and introduced the Premier variant, Holden’s first ever luxury model, but it kept the old suspension and the 138 cubic inch (2.3 liter) “Grey” straight-six with a measly 75 bhp. Holden built 154,811 EJs in 13 months, it sold well, but it was clear that a new model was needed to stay competitive with their arch rivals over at Australia’s Ford operations.

The new EH sedan changed far more of that body than Holden’s earlier facelifts had. The roof, rear quarters, trunk, front fenders, hood, grille and tail lights were all brand new, giving a squarer profile, though the ute and panel van kept the older EJ tail lights. The Standard EH sedan remained at the EJ’s price, but it offered a lot more car for the money.

The new straight-six took its nickname from the bright red color of its block . It was a fresh design rather than a development of the earlier Grey six, a pushrod overhead-valve unit with seven main bearings and a single-barrel Bendix-Stromberg carburetor, built in two sizes on a common 3.00 inch stroke. The 149 cubic inch (2.4 liter) version made 100 bhp at 4,400 rpm and 145 lb ft of torque at 2,000 rpm, with a 95 bhp low-compression alternative.

Opening the bore from 3.25 to 3.563 inches gave the 179 cubic inch (2.9 liter) engine 115 bhp at 4,000 rpm and 175 lb ft of torque at 1,600 rpm, 53% more power than the Grey with a much stronger bottom end to boot.

raw_title: Why The Toyota Hilux Is One Of The Most Legendary Compact Trucks Ever Built
title: Why The Toyota Hilux Is One Of The Most Legendary Compact Trucks Ever Built
raw_summary: You'd probably agree that there aren't many brands with a reputation for building long-lasting cars like Toyota's . And within the Japanese automaker's lineup sits a pickup truck that, although fairly unpopular stateside, enjoys legendary status elsewhere around the globe: the Toyota Hilux. It's almost impossible to talk about the Hilux and not mention Top Gear's elaborate little excursion, which played quite a significant role in lending the compact truck its "indestructible" title. Even after subjecting it to many grueling events, including setting it on fire and drowning it in seawater, the Hilux simply refused to die, only needing a few basic tools and a bit of mechanical sympathy to get it running again. You may have also seen James May drive one up an active volcano, which was the same Hilux the camera crew used while filming the Polar Special, where he accompanied Jeremy Clarkson in their expedition to the North Pole — also in a Hilux.

article_paragraphs: You'd probably agree that there aren't many brands with a reputation for building long-lasting cars like Toyota's . And within the Japanese automaker's lineup sits a pickup truck that, although fairly unpopular stateside, enjoys legendary status elsewhere around the globe: the Toyota Hilux.

It's almost impossible to talk about the Hilux and not mention Top Gear's elaborate little excursion, which played quite a significant role in lending the compact truck its "indestructible" title. Even after subjecting it to many grueling events, including setting it on fire and drowning it in seawater, the Hilux simply refused to die, only needing a few basic tools and a bit of mechanical sympathy to get it running again. You may have also seen James May drive one up an active volcano, which was the same Hilux the camera crew used while filming the Polar Special, where he accompanied Jeremy Clarkson in their expedition to the North Pole — also in a Hilux.

Beyond television, the pickup is also known for being a trusty little companion on actual battlefields. The infamous "Toyota War," which essentially took place in the Saharan desert, saw Chad deploy several Hilux pickups during its conflict with Libya in the mid-1980s. The pickup also has quite the following in Australia, a place known for its tough terrain and demanding conditions. In the last decade or so, Toyota managed to shift over half a million units of the truck in Australia alone, making it the country's best-selling vehicle during that period.

Suffice it to say, its robust ladder-frame build, relative simplicity, and ease of repair, combined with Toyota's reputation, Top Gear's many indestructibility stunts, and the truck's overall reliability — even across the harshest of environments — all lend the Hilux its status.

The legend is only amplified when you realize Toyota sells the Hilux in over 190 countries and regions around the world. For context, there are between 193 and 237 countries in the world, depending on whether you factor in disputed zones and regions with full or partial sovereignty. Despite Toyota shipping it to almost every part of the globe, one country where the Hilux is not sold is the United States. Even though the pickup was available this side of the pond, it bore the "Toyota Truck" moniker for most of its time on U.S. soil, having bid farewell in 1995 to make way for the Toyota Tacoma. As far as Toyota was concerned, the Tacoma, being slightly larger and offering different powertrain choices, seemed like a much better fit for American customer preferences.

Besides, the Chicken Tax still exists, which, if you weren't aware, is a 25% tariff levied on light trucks imported to the U.S. So, if Toyota wanted to bring the latest ninth-generation Hilux to U.S. shores, it'd have to put up with the tariffs (and possibly worry about internal competition), or build them locally or somewhere like Mexico or Canada, where the company might qualify for preferential tariff treatment. Bear in mind, the Hilux is already manufactured in numerous countries around the world, including Argentina, Venezuela, India, Pakistan, and Thailand, as well as five other locations across Asia and Africa.

Moreover, Toyota is reportedly working on a compact truck based on the Corolla . According to Car and Driver , it might be called the Stout or something simple as the Corolla Pickup. Although details are slim, the chances of that truck filling the compact space seem much higher than the Hilux arriving stateside.

title: 7 Naturally Aspirated 4-Cylinder Engines That Pump Out V6 And Even V8 Power
raw_summary: Naturally aspirated combustion engines. Aren't they just exquisite? Nothing sends a tingle down your spine like a V12 at full tilt, and one could argue that the only thing that works harder than a free-breathing V8 is Dwight Schrute. V6s, meanwhile, are just about as versatile as inventions come, powering everything from the glorious Alfa Romeo 155 DTM to the humble Honda Odyssey. Then there's the four-cylinder engine. It is by far the most successful of the bunch, and though it isn't quite as exotic or exciting as its peers, it can pack an almighty punch under the right hood. That is precisely what we want to celebrate in this article: the rowdiest, most powerful little naturally aspirated four-bangers ever created. We've got road cars, race cars, and even a reborn 1970s legend making appearances, and some of these would be more than capable of scaring a V6 or two (which would make, er, a V12). Saddle up — the first one's a corker.

Then there's the four-cylinder engine. It is by far the most successful of the bunch, and though it isn't quite as exotic or exciting as its peers, it can pack an almighty punch under the right hood. That is precisely what we want to celebrate in this article: the rowdiest, most powerful little naturally aspirated four-bangers ever created. We've got road cars, race cars, and even a reborn 1970s legend making appearances, and some of these would be more than capable of scaring a V6 or two (which would make, er, a V12). Saddle up — the first one's a corker.

Take 1,224 pounds, spread almost perfectly between the axles, and add a 343-hp, 2.5-liter naturally aspirated four-cylinder. Sounds like quite the recipe, doesn't it? The Mono R delivers precisely the sort of statistical hit squad you'd imagine: 0 to 62 mph in 2.5 seconds and a top speed of 170 mph. Oh, and that engine also spins to a wicked 8,800 rpm – and since the only gearbox option is a six-speed sequential, you can really max those revs out before upshifting.

More numbers, did you say? Sure. The Mono R develops 137 hp per liter, which trumps even the Porsche 918 Spyder hypercar. It also delivers a power-to-weight ratio of 618 hp per metric ton, superior even to the unhinged Lamborghini Sesto Elemento. All this helped BAC set a new production-car lap record at the Red Bull Ring in Austria, beating the previous leader, the Ferrari LaFerrari, by almost 6 seconds.

Widely considered to be one of the finest two-seat driver's cars ever made, the Honda S2000 is nothing short of a mechanical masterpiece. Its engine is a screamer: two liters, four cylinders, and a bit of VTEC wizardry sprinkled on top, culminating in a 9,000-rpm redline. The F22C1 engine in the S2000 may have been unique to the U.S. , but it wasn't the cream of the crop.

That accolade goes to the original F20C, which produced 247 hp (as opposed to 237 hp). Small margins, sure, but the F20C's specific output of 123 hp per liter remained a record for naturally aspirated production engines for about a decade. It was eventually dethroned by the stunning Ferrari 458 Italia, and in truth, there's nothing to be upset about there. Here's a fun fact for you: at its redline, the S2000's engine had a mean piston speed of 4,960 feet per minute (25.2 meters per second), which was even more than what in-period Formula 1 engines could manage.

These days, the E30 M3 is riding high as a cult icon whose design speaks to almost everybody it passes, but back in the late 1980s and early 1990s, it had absolutely no problem getting those perfectly symmetrical kidney grilles dirty.

In its first two seasons in touring car racing, the E30 M3 won titles in England, France, and Germany, and even became a world champion. In fact, during its five-year racing career in Group A, the E30 M3 is estimated to have won more than 1,400 races worldwide. That averages out to one race win every 31 hours.

article_paragraphs: A dramatic Mexican Grand Prix Formula 1 qualifying session left us scrabbling for enough ‘winners’ for our regular winner and losers list - with only a few people overperforming and plenty ruing missed chances.
Lewis Hamilton always had faith that Ferrari had a car in Mexico that could take pole position – but knew that delivering it would be another matter.
So after a 2026 season where time and again Ferrari has failed to nail those final laps in Q3, Hamilton was clearly overjoyed to have delivered his first grand prix pole for the Prancing Horse.
It also made the 41-year-old F1’s oldest polesitter since Mario Andretti took that famous top spot at Monza in 1982 aged 42.

Hamilton said the key to performing today was getting the tyres working and nailing the balance perfectly throughout the lap – as the shifting temperatures of the fronts and rears altered performance all around the circuit.
Hamilton likened nailing that balance to “finding a needle in a haystack” – which is why he reckoned being millimetre perfect was essential for him to have pulled off his pole feat. - Jon Noble
Precious few weekends have promised much at all for Fernando Alonso this season. Mexico, relatively speaking, did: 12th in FP2, 14th in FP3.

It’s about as good as it’s got for the Aston Martin driver as Honda seemed to be managing the unique Mexico challenge well. Alonso even had the brief joy of briefly going quickest after almost half the grid had set a laptime in Q1!

article_paragraphs: Liam Lawson has lost his top-10 start for Formula 1’s Mexican Grand Prix over a technical infringement.

Lawson qualified eighth-fastest at Mexico City though would start ninth at best due to a one-place grid penalty picked up for his needless clash with Max Verstappen in Friday practice - which he has apologised to Verstappen for.
But he was then reported for a breach of F1’s complex MGU-K power deployment rules just after finishing his final lap in Q2.
Technical breaches are usually a black-and-white matter that result in disqualification - and that duly occurred later on Saturday evening.

Lawson and Racing Bulls were summoned because “the driver maximum power demand and the electrical DC power of the [MGU-K] were reduced at greater rates than what is permitted”, according to FIA F1 technical delegate Jo Bauer.
Essentially, when the Q2 lap ended, Lawson’s car lost all electric power deployment too suddenly.
The battery-powered MGU-K adds up to 350kW on top of the engine but when that boost has to end the rules don’t let it switch off in one go.
It has to fade out gradually, by no more than 50kW or 100kW each second depending on the track. A full cut takes several seconds.

title: 7 V8s With A Reputation For Being Nearly Indestructible
raw_summary: Who doesn't like the raw power offered by a V8, if you can afford the gas, that is? But it's not just the horsepower that draws so many of us to these engines. Some V8s are among the longest-lasting engines on the road today. There are multiple examples of drivers taking their V8-equipped vehicles, especially pickups, over a million miles. That's quite the feat. Some examples of these million-mile accomplishments include a 1UZ-FE 4.0-equipped Lexus LS 400 that already had nearly 900,000 miles on the odometer when it was bought by a Road & Track writer for the express purpose of taking over a million. There are a couple of examples of owners driving another Toyota V8 engine, the 2UZ-FE 4.7, past the million-mile mark. Other examples include Frank Oresnik who drove his 1991 Chevy Silverado, which featured a small-block Chevy 350, over a million miles. David Mueller did the same thing with his 2002 F-350 Super Duty.

article_paragraphs: Who doesn't like the raw power offered by a V8, if you can afford the gas, that is? But it's not just the horsepower that draws so many of us to these engines. Some V8s are among the longest-lasting engines on the road today. There are multiple examples of drivers taking their V8-equipped vehicles, especially pickups, over a million miles. That's quite the feat.

Some examples of these million-mile accomplishments include a 1UZ-FE 4.0-equipped Lexus LS 400 that already had nearly 900,000 miles on the odometer when it was bought by a Road & Track writer for the express purpose of taking over a million. There are a couple of examples of owners driving another Toyota V8 engine, the 2UZ-FE 4.7, past the million-mile mark. Other examples include Frank Oresnik who drove his 1991 Chevy Silverado, which featured a small-block Chevy 350, over a million miles. David Mueller did the same thing with his 2002 F-350 Super Duty.

An engine doesn't have to go a million miles to demonstrate its durability, though. The Ford 4.6-liter Modular 2-valve took all kinds of use and abuse as the standard engine used in Crown Victoria Police Interceptors during the 1990s and 2000s, and could still go for hundreds of thousands of miles. Then there's GM's Vortec 8100, an engine so rugged that it was not only put in Chevy and GMC trucks, but also in boats and RVs. There was also the versatile Chrysler LA 318, which earned the reputation of being "bulletproof."

Lexus debuted its first model in 1989, and no doubt wanted its relatively new luxury brand to be associated with sophistication and comfort, but that would require worthy engines with high-end performance. Enter the 1UZ-FE 4.0, an aluminum block, oversquare 4.0-liter V8, with four camshafts and 32 valves. The 1UZ displaced 3,969 cc, with an 87.5 x 82.5 mm bore and stroke. It made around 250 horsepower and 260 lb-ft of torque, not exactly earth-shattering in our modern turbocharged era, but not too shabby for 1989. In fact, this engine is often described as "overengineered".

The vehicle it would be matched with, the Lexus LS 400, had its own share of overengineering. Born from a billion-dollar secret project at Toyota , it spent six years in development and went through eight proposals for its final design. There were 50 clay models, about 450 vehicle prototypes, and 1.67 million miles of testing.

All of that testing and engineering paid off. One person who could bear witness to the near indestructibility of this engine is Matt Farah from Road & Track . He was presented with the opportunity to buy a 1996 Lexus LS 400 with 897,000 miles on it. Farah acquired it with the goal of taking it over 1,000,000 miles. After four years of driving it himself, as well as lending it out to friends, acquaintances, and people he didn't even know, he reached the goal of putting seven digits on the original engine.

Toyota followed up the 1UZ with the 2UZ-FE 4.7 , but this engine wasn't to be put into a luxury sedan. Built with a rugged cast-iron block, it was meant to last through wear and abuse as it powered large SUVs and pickup trucks. A 2003 Land Cruiser Amazon equipped with this engine could crank out 235 hp and 320 lb-ft of torque with a 9:6:1 compression ratio. It wasn't breaking any records in the power department, but it was a good engine, nonetheless. The 2UZ-FE 4.7 would go on to be featured in the Tundra, Sequoia, LX 470, and GX 470.

Several years ago, Louisiana man Aaron Morvant drove his 2UZ-FE-equipped 2007 Toyota Tundra past the million-mile mark. In fact, he had bought the truck to use as a contract hot shot driver, specifically because of Toyota's reputation for reliability. (Toyotas make up the majority of our list of vehicles you can expect to drive for 300,000 miles .) The truck as still running great after a million miles, in spite of being banged up.

raw_title: Why The Hyundai Tucson Loses Almost 7 Cubic Feet Of Cargo Space In PHEV Form
title: The Hidden Flaw: Why The Hyundai Tucson Loses 7 Cubic Feet Of Cargo Space
raw_summary: The current Hyundai Tucson compact crossover is available with a pure gas, regular hybrid, or a plug-in hybrid powertrain . If you need every last inch of cargo room, however, the fuel-efficient plug-in may not be the best choice because its cargo area is smaller by almost seven cubic feet. The reason is fairly obvious for those familiar with how electrified cars are built. It's because it has to accommodate the hybrid battery. Per the official Hyundai specs, the internal combustion and hybrid versions of the 2026 Tucson both have 38.7 cubic feet of SAE-approved cargo room behind the second row of seats. The PHEV, however, has 31.9 cubes, a delta of precisely 6.8 cubic feet or almost 18%. For what we suspect is the same reason, the plug-in hybrid Tucson also gets 1.8 inches less rear legroom than the other Tucsons, measuring 39.5 inches instead of 41.3.

For what it's worth, Hyundai has already unveiled and is preparing to launch the all-new fifth-gen 2027 Tucson . In certain markets, that one will also be available in three powertrains: gas, hybrid, and plug-in. The latter, however, won't be sold in North America, reportedly due to low demand. On paper, though, the new U.S.-spec Tucson will apparently be bigger than the current one, boasting 41.7 cubic feet of cargo room per Hyundai's current literature.

In fairness to the current-gen Tucson PHEV, that lithium-ion battery packs 13.8 kWh worth of energy, delivering 32 miles of electric-only range. And, for what it's worth, the plug-in makes 268 total system horsepower compared to the 231 of the regular hybrid and 187 of the gas. If you're about that part-time EV life, seven or so cubic feet of cargo room feels like a small price to pay. Speaking of which, the 2026 Hyundai Tucson starts at $31,350, while the plug-in version goes for $42,325.

title: How Semi-Truck Fleets Are Slashing Diesel Costs With Radical Aerodynamics
raw_summary: Diesel fuel prices reached a new record high in early September , and they kept on climbing until September 21 this year. At its highest, the average price of a gallon of diesel reached $6.53. And while things have dropped since then, it's still at $6.27 per gallon as of writing this article. The number then topped $140 billion by October 21, and nearly $63 billion of that had come from the especially high costs of diesel. article_paragraphs: Diesel fuel prices reached a new record high in early September , and they kept on climbing until September 21 this year. At its highest, the average price of a gallon of diesel reached $6.53. And while things have dropped since then, it's still at $6.27 per gallon as of writing this article. Further, the Republican war to make gas more expensive seems to be working, as it had cost Americans more than $100 billion at the pump through early September. The number then topped $140 billion by October 21, and nearly $63 billion of that had come from the especially high costs of diesel.

With that in mind, some truckers are turning to new hardware to help get a few more miles out of each tank. For example, the folks at FlowBelow – headquartered in Round Rock, Texas — recently introduced the Trailer AeroSlider kit that promises fuel savings of 2.5% by improving a truck's aerodynamics. The company claims that this works out to saving 3 gallons of fuel for every 1,000 miles traveled.

Now, that may not seem like a lot at first glance, but think of it this way: The typical Class 8 truck travels about 58,890 miles per year, according to the U.S. Department of Energy , meaning the new device would save roughly 176.7 gallons of diesel every year. With diesel at $6.27 per gallon, that comes out to about $1,107 per truck. A long-haul trucker who covers 125,000 miles annually could save $2,350 per year. For the very few fleets above 100 trucks –- representing only 0.7% of all commercial carriers (via FleetOwner ) -– savings could soar into six-figure territory. As for exactly how the Trailer AeroSlider does its job, that comes next.

The first thing you need to know is that semi-truck trailers can have single or dual rear axles , and they don't have to be fixed in place. With double axles specifically, they're often part of a sliding tandem, which is basically a single unit that incorporates both axles. Drivers can then slide it toward the front or back of the trailer along rails attached to the bottom of the trailer frame for optimum weight distribution on the axles. The main pieces from the Trailer AeroSlider kit are lightweight fairings, or panels, that attach one per side to the suspension part of the sliding tandem — immediately behind the rear-most wheels. Because of this, drivers don't have to separately reposition the fairings if they reposition the slider as a whole.

The panels themselves are oriented so that their surfaces are parallel to the sides of the trailer. In other words, they're essentially smaller versions of aerodynamic trailer skirts that are tailored specifically to reduce drag from wind flowing around the trailer's wheels and suspension. The AeroSlider package includes both a pair of panels along with two flow-through mud flaps and four of the company's aero wheel covers – all of which must be installed to achieve the 3-gallons-per-1,000-miles benchmark.

The whole setup can be installed in 45 minutes, and it only adds about 30 lbs of weight to the truck. The AeroSlider kit starts from $320, meaning it should theoretically pay for itself in a matter of months. FlowBelow puts the icing on the cake by making the system compatible with most other aero-style trailer upgrades and most wheel/tire combinations.

raw_title: YouTuber Invents Device That Hides License Plates From Flock Cameras
title: YouTuber Builds Stealth Shield That Blinds Police Flock Surveillance Cameras
raw_summary: Flock cameras take an unimaginably huge number of pictures of cars and license plates, creating a searchable database of times and locations that can be used to track your movements. If you don't care to participate, you can use apps like MapQuest to avoid these cameras , or FlockHopper to automatically route around them. Or you can do as YouTuber Studio Hotrods did, and design a system to make your license plate invisible, but only near a Flock camera. What Studio Hotrods came up with is a clever system that obscures your plate only when you're in view of a Flock camera. The video goes into detail, but basically, an Arduino computer controls a piece of smart glass that's clear when it receives power but turns opaque when the power shuts off. This smart glass goes over the license plate.

article_paragraphs: Flock cameras take an unimaginably huge number of pictures of cars and license plates, creating a searchable database of times and locations that can be used to track your movements. If you don't care to participate, you can use apps like MapQuest to avoid these cameras , or FlockHopper to automatically route around them. Or you can do as YouTuber Studio Hotrods did, and design a system to make your license plate invisible, but only near a Flock camera.

What Studio Hotrods came up with is a clever system that obscures your plate only when you're in view of a Flock camera. The video goes into detail, but basically, an Arduino computer controls a piece of smart glass that's clear when it receives power but turns opaque when the power shuts off. This smart glass goes over the license plate.

The Arduino is also connected to a GPS antenna and module that tells it the vehicle's location, which it cross-references with an SD card containing a database of Flock camera locations, likely by the DeFlock mapping project . Under normal driving conditions, the smart glass receives power and remains clear, keeping the license plate visible as is legally required. When the vehicle passes a Flock camera, however, it briefly turns the smart glass opaque, just long enough to prevent the camera from scanning the plate.

This seems like a pretty neat idea. Unless a cop is looking right at your license plate at the moment you pass a Flock camera, they're still going to see your plate, so there shouldn't be a problem, right? Unfortunately, it's not as simple as that.

According to Allowed Here , every state has some kind of restriction on license plate covers. They are illegal in eight states, including Illinois, where the car used for testing in this video is registered. States that haven't banned covers outright still require the plate to be legible, and they may not obscure the plate in any way. Depending on where you live, you could still get pulled over just for having a cover on your license plate, even if it's as clear as glass at the time.

States are already cracking down on license plate flippers , which obscure plates both from cops and automatic toll cameras. Studio Hotrods' "Flock-O-Matic" system recognizes these valid reasons, which is why it keeps the plate visible unless you're in direct view of a Flock camera. But the law doesn't care what your intentions are, only that the plate can't be obscured. Plus, it's easy to skip the Arduino and turn the smart glass clear and opaque manually, blocking your plate anytime you want. Cops don't generally like that.

While Studio Hotrods is designing, testing, and even working on a patent for this device, it's not selling it at this time. A hobbyist with some programming skill could probably figure out how to make something similar — for testing purposes only, of course. In many places, using it on the street is likely to get you the very attention you're trying to avoid.

raw_title: These Are The Reasons You Are Keeping Old Cars On The Road
title: Why Real Drivers Refuse To Give Up Keeping Old Cars On The Road
raw_summary: When times are tough the Jalopnik commenter section toughens up. With the economic future of this country, perhaps the world, up in the air, it's getting more and more difficult to justify the expense of a new car and the related payments and high insurance costs. Last weekend I asked all of you to chime in with your stories of keeping an old car on the road to avoid the costs of a new car. I guess I shouldn't have been surprised that many of you have chosen to keep old cars on the road for non-economic reasons as well. Most of the responses boiled down to not being able to afford a new car, or being able to afford one but unwilling to buy for a variety of reasons. Lately I've seen quite a lot of chatter on the internet about a preference for older automobiles. Whether it's for cost, simplicity, maintenance, driving enjoyment, or tactile non-touch-screen interiors, it's become a common refrain. "Buy a pre-financial crisis car and maintain it for the rest of your life," the peanut gallery mumbles. I've always been a fan of older cars, whether out of economic necessity, or a desire for something with a sense of occasion, so I find myself agreeing with them.

raw_title: These Are 10 Of The Most Notable Ford F-150 Changes
title: 10 Most Shocking Changes Coming To The Ford F-150 Changes
raw_summary: The Ford F-150 just got a mild refresh for 2027 , and the changes are quite minimal compared to the current model. This has not always been the case, since the Blue Oval company has not exactly shied away from experimentation with the F-150 in the past. Ford had been making trucks for a long time, but in the period after the Second World War, the company branded its light-duty trucks as the "F-series" from 1948. Initially, the Ford truck lineup was broken down into the F-1, F-2, and F-3, to represent the half-ton, three-quarter-ton, and one-ton units, respectively. Ford also made progressively heavier trucks right up until the F-8 designation. In '53, the naming for the light trucks was changed to the F-100, F-250, and F-350 for the half-ton, three-quarter-ton, and one-ton rigs, respectively. The F-150 name wouldn't arrive till 1975. Additionally, Ford transitioned the truck line from the legendary flathead engines to the Y-block overhead valve (OHV) V8s between 1953 and 1954, starting with the 239-cubic-inch V8, followed by a 272-cubic-inch V8 from 1956 onward. The trucks were then redesigned in 1957, 1961, 1967, and 1973 – during this time, the F-series lineup gradually began losing its curves and adopting a squarer, flatter design and fascia. As part of these changes, Ford bounced around between chassis redevelopments and styling updates, offered creature comforts, and introduced new engine choices. For one model year (1956), we also got a fully wrap-around windshield. In 1965, a new trim called the "Ranger" was also introduced, and the I-beam suspension was also introduced that year.
summary: The Ford F-150 just got a mild refresh for 2027 , and the changes are quite minimal compared to the current model. This has not always been the case, since the Blue Oval company has not exactly shied away from experimentation with the F-150 in the past.
article_paragraphs: The Ford F-150 just got a mild refresh for 2027 , and the changes are quite minimal compared to the current model. This has not always been the case, since the Blue Oval company has not exactly shied away from experimentation with the F-150 in the past. Ford had been making trucks for a long time, but in the period after the Second World War, the company branded its light-duty trucks as the "F-series" from 1948. Initially, the Ford truck lineup was broken down into the F-1, F-2, and F-3, to represent the half-ton, three-quarter-ton, and one-ton units, respectively. Ford also made progressively heavier trucks right up until the F-8 designation. In '53, the naming for the light trucks was changed to the F-100, F-250, and F-350 for the half-ton, three-quarter-ton, and one-ton rigs, respectively. The F-150 name wouldn't arrive till 1975.

Additionally, Ford transitioned the truck line from the legendary flathead engines to the Y-block overhead valve (OHV) V8s between 1953 and 1954, starting with the 239-cubic-inch V8, followed by a 272-cubic-inch V8 from 1956 onward. The trucks were then redesigned in 1957, 1961, 1967, and 1973 – during this time, the F-series lineup gradually began losing its curves and adopting a squarer, flatter design and fascia. As part of these changes, Ford bounced around between chassis redevelopments and styling updates, offered creature comforts, and introduced new engine choices. For one model year (1956), we also got a fully wrap-around windshield. In 1965, a new trim called the "Ranger" was also introduced, and the I-beam suspension was also introduced that year.

In 1975, Ford came out with the F-150 (1976 model pictured above), which had a heavier gross vehicle weight rating (GVWR) than FoMoCo's other half-ton truck, the F-100. This let the F-150 skirt around emission loopholes, allowing the half-ton truck to be sold without catalytic converters, which the F-100 needed to have. You see, in 1975, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) used to classify vehicles with a GVWR of under 6,000 pounds as being "light-duty" trucks, and in 1975, light duty trucks had to use unleaded fuel and needed cats.

Ford opted to equip the then-new F-150 with beefier components, giving it a GVWR of 6,050 pounds, compared to the F-100's 5,700 maximum, pushing it past the 6,000-pound threshold by a hair. Additionally, it's worth noting that the original 1975 F-150 only came as a 2WD vehicle, though 4WD was added just a year later, in 1976. And yes, the F-100 doggedly remained on as a model all the way until the 1983 year, which meant that for the better part of a decade, Ford was offering two half-ton trucks.

In '83, the Ford Ranger was introduced (as its own model, not as a trim like it was earlier), and thus, the F-150 completely replaced the F-100 – by then, the F-150 had taken on most of that classic square body shape that we all know and love. The rest, as they say, is history, with the Ford F-150 eventually becoming the best-selling new vehicle in 20 states .

In 1980, the entire lineup got an overhaul. Fun fact: The Ford trucks from 1980 were called "Bullnose" models by some, because of the grille's taper. During the 1980 redesign of the lineup, FoMoCo completely reworked the chassis, making the new trucks lighter. One of the ways in which this was accomplished was by drilling holes into the chassis. However, this "Swiss cheese frame" would later revert to a solid chassis from 1982. Furthermore, the 1980 redesign gave the 4WD models twin traction beam suspension. Essentially, there were two traction beams running inward — one from each wheel (hence, "twin") — while each wheel had a coil for suspension.

The differential was mounted on the driver side traction beam, and not in the middle like on solid axle units. The 2WD models retained the twin I-beam suspensions in the front, and a solid axle at the rear. That twin I-beam setup had roots going all the way back to 1965, which is when the system was first introduced. For the 1980 redesign, the F-150s continued to use Ford's 9-inch rear axle, while the twin traction beam was from Dana. From 1980 to 1982, the 9-incher was standard, but the 8.8 began making its way into the F-150 from '83. To figure out which axle your truck has, look at the differential cover – 9-inch axles have no cover, whereas 8.8s have a 10-bolt one. It's a shame, because the Ford 9-Inch rear end really still is America's favorite axle .

Starting in 1985, Ford began offering electronic fuel injection — EFI, for short — on the F-150. Initially, EFI tech was offered on the 302-cubic-inch (or 5.0 liter) V8, which bumped power to about 225 horsepower on the high-output version of that engine. By around 1987, the F-150 ditched carbs across the lineup. For trucks made during the period, the F-150 received a few aesthetic changes, chief of which included rounding out of the wheel arches — which were formerly square-ish — and the headlights now sitting flush with the grille.

raw_title: Could The Original Jaguar E-Type Really Do 150 MPH?
title: Busting The Myth: Could The Original Jaguar E-Type Actually Hit 150 MPH?
raw_summary: A top speed of 150 miles per hour is achievable by many reasonably powerful cars these days. If we consider EVs, it gets more absurd. Even the seven-seat Lucid Gravity SUV can do the 0 to 150 mph run three seconds quicker than a Corvette Z06 . However, in the 1960s, a 150 mph run meant something entirely different — think of the 1968 Dodge Charger R/T Hemi or the Shelby Cobra 427. Even among sports cars and exotics, the 1960 Ferrari 250 GT Coupé maxed out at 140 mph, while the Aston Martin DB4GT topped out at 153 mph, and the 1960s Porsche 911T reached 124 mph. At the top end of the market, the fastest cars, like the Lamborghini Miura or the Ferrari 365 GTB/4, could hit about 174 mph. The absolute top end belonged to the 1969 Dodge Charger Daytona, which lapped Talladega at over 200 mph in 1970, though the car that did it was a Chrysler development test car. The Jaguar E-Type, one of the most alluring cars from the 1960s, is cited as a 150 mph car from the factory, but is that really the case?

article_paragraphs: A top speed of 150 miles per hour is achievable by many reasonably powerful cars these days. If we consider EVs, it gets more absurd. Even the seven-seat Lucid Gravity SUV can do the 0 to 150 mph run three seconds quicker than a Corvette Z06 . However, in the 1960s, a 150 mph run meant something entirely different — think of the 1968 Dodge Charger R/T Hemi or the Shelby Cobra 427.

Even among sports cars and exotics, the 1960 Ferrari 250 GT Coupé maxed out at 140 mph, while the Aston Martin DB4GT topped out at 153 mph, and the 1960s Porsche 911T reached 124 mph. At the top end of the market, the fastest cars, like the Lamborghini Miura or the Ferrari 365 GTB/4, could hit about 174 mph. The absolute top end belonged to the 1969 Dodge Charger Daytona, which lapped Talladega at over 200 mph in 1970, though the car that did it was a Chrysler development test car. The Jaguar E-Type, one of the most alluring cars from the 1960s, is cited as a 150 mph car from the factory, but is that really the case?

According to Autocar , the 150 mph figure came from press cars, not showroom ones. The coupé Autocar tested (9600 HP) recorded 150 mph at Jabbeke, Belgium. Another publication, The Motor (which later became part of Autocar), drove a roadster (77 RW) and managed it in one direction only. Autocar's retrospective notes 9600 HP's gas-flowed head and states: "Not that standard E-types would have reached 150." So the claim is real, but the story is complicated.

Autocar's 9600 HP recorded 150.4 mph and a 0 to 60 mph time of 6.9 seconds, while The Motor's roadster (77 RW) managed 149 mph and 7.1 seconds. Both ran on Dunlop R5 racing tires and, most importantly, Autocar 's own history says 9600 HP was "most likely specially prepared for those tests."

So, what does "specially prepared" mean in this case? Well, 9600 HP's XK150S engine had a gas-flowed head, adding about 20 to 25 bhp. In 1994, Motor Sport Magazine 's Bill Boddy, who had also tested the car, reported a claim that 9600 HP had a "D-type racing cylinder head, valve gear and breathers."

Later cars followed a similar pattern. As recounted by AROnline , The Motor's 4.2-liter E-Type coupé (ARW 732B) reached only 148 mph in its 1964 test. Jaguar then took the car back, and the published figure became 150 mph. On that same car, 5,000 rpm equaled 130 mph, so 150 mph would have needed close to 6,000 rpm. In May 1965, Autocar took another coupé (AWK 349B) to 153 mph on Dunlop R6 racing tires.

So what could a normal car do? Maurice Smith, one of the Autocar testers of 9600 HP, later owned a 3.8 roadster and put its best speed at 137 mph. Motor Sport writer Denis Jenkinson's 4.2 coupé reached 143 mph on an Italian autostrada, though with a lower-compression engine. In 2015, a driver took a restored production coupé (chassis 860001) to 146.49 mph on a German autobahn. In the real world, a standard E-Type would top out at around 137 to 146 mph.

Nowadays, Jaguar is busy with cars like the 2028 Jaguar Type 01 , a fully electric four-door GT with up to 1,015 horsepower and a clear goal of being noticed. Back in the 1960s, things were a little different. The E-Type was introduced at the Geneva Motor Show in 1961, and the moment it came out, it captivated the industry. Rumor has it that Enzo Ferrari himself called it the most beautiful car ever made.

title: Why You Might Need To Use Neutral On An Automatic Transmission
raw_summary: Automatic transmissions may not be the enthusiast choice , but they are good at removing some of the stress and confusion from driving. There's no tricky clutch to balance, and no mystery over which gear you should select for that upcoming curve. Sure, some have manual modes with paddles and a Sport setting. But their use is optional. Most drivers likely just drop the shifter into drive, and away they go. There is though, one feature on automatic transmissions that might cause confusion, even now, more than 70 years after clutch pedals began to disappear from American cars. Why do automatic shifters have a neutral position, and when would you ever need to use it? Conventional automatics are built from sets of planetary gears, and use a fluid coupling called a torque converter to multiply engine torque and transfer it to the wheels.

article_paragraphs: Automatic transmissions may not be the enthusiast choice , but they are good at removing some of the stress and confusion from driving. There's no tricky clutch to balance, and no mystery over which gear you should select for that upcoming curve. Sure, some have manual modes with paddles and a Sport setting. But their use is optional. Most drivers likely just drop the shifter into drive, and away they go.

There is though, one feature on automatic transmissions that might cause confusion, even now, more than 70 years after clutch pedals began to disappear from American cars. Why do automatic shifters have a neutral position, and when would you ever need to use it? Conventional automatics are built from sets of planetary gears, and use a fluid coupling called a torque converter to multiply engine torque and transfer it to the wheels.

Dual-clutch automatics are more like traditional manual transmissions, but with two electronically-controlled clutches, one for odd gears, and another for evens. A continuously variable transmission (CVT) — which is not as bad as everyone thinks — relies on a belt running between two cone-shaped pulleys to create an almost infinite number of gear ratios. You can't stall any of them in normal driving when the powertrain is working correctly, but shifting to neutral has the same effect it would in a manual car. It fully disconnects the engine torque from the driven wheels.

That ability to separate the engine from the wheels can be useful if you need to move an automatic car around a workshop when the engine won't fire up. Or if you need to tow it out of a ditch. But you should never tow a traditional automatic car too far with the engine off and the drive wheels on the ground. The transmission relies on a flow of fluid to protect its components from wear, and if the engine isn't running, the transmission pump isn't either.

You might also find yourself grateful for that neutral position if your throttle jams wide open , a thankfully rare occurrence. Shifting to N means you could regain some control because the brakes aren't battling against the powertrain's determination to rendezvous with the horizon. Switching the engine off is an option too, but then you could lose the brake booster and steering assistance, which sounds even worse.

What about shifting to neutral when idling? Engineers say there's no point. It saves almost no fuel and the additional shifts between drive and neutral can add unnecessary wear. Same applies when you're going downhill. You'll save little gas, and have less control over the car. Another Neutral no-no is when parking. Experts say you should always use park, instead of slotting neutral and relying on the parking brake. Park engages a pawl that locks the transmission's output shaft, and provides an extra layer of protection against rollaway accidents. All of which means neutral is somewhere most of us will only spend time on our way from drive to reverse and back again.

raw_title: Why We As Enthusiasts Accept The Risk Of Driving Old, Unsafe Cars
title: Why Passionate Gearheads Gladly Risk Driving Dangerous Classic Cars
raw_summary: They just don't make them like they used to . That old saw is true of many things, but perhaps it applies most to cars. Modern cars are empirically better in practically every measure of statistics. Not only are modern SUVs quicker, faster, and more powerful than pretty much any sports car from decades gone by, but they're safer, quieter, and more comfortable. Old cars can't touch a modern car when it comes to convenience features, incredible audio, or efficiency. It's hard to find a metric by which anyone would want an old car over something new. Old cars don't have the safety systems, crash structures, or even airbags that are mandatory these days. Driving an old car in today's traffic requires a leap of faith and a stroke of luck, because it's simply more dangerous than driving a newfangled computer-controlled crash contraption. Self-induced crashes are more likely in an old car, and you're much less likely to survive that crash in an old car. A Department of Transportation study found that crashes in vehicles over 20 years old were about 80% more likely to be fatal than similar crashes in new vehicles.

Self-induced crashes are more likely in an old car, and you're much less likely to survive that crash in an old car. A Department of Transportation study found that crashes in vehicles over 20 years old were about 80% more likely to be fatal than similar crashes in new vehicles.

Why do we drive them if they're more dangerous? There are so many reasons that humans do anything with old cars. We're going to examine two of the primary reasons why we keep old cars around. There are more secondary and tertiary reasons like nostalgia , design , finances , tradition, heritage, and craftsmanship, but I think chances are you drive a vintage automobile simply because you're seeking a thrill or you want to be part of an in-crowd group . I posit almost all of vintage car culture boils down to these two motivating factors.

Vintage cars have a certain feel that can't be matched. When you attune to an old car, you get a level of connectedness and an airy laissaiz-faire flow that hasn't been available with new cars for at least thirty years. Many enthusiasts enjoy the process of building rapport with their vintage automobile. Compared to a modern car, even a modern sports car, something with an anachronistic touch just adds a level of artful emotionality that practically nothing built in the digital era can match.

There is certainly a level of thrill seeker to the vintage car enthusiast, not driven by the danger but "sensation-seeking" behavior. The danger is part of the fun, but not the driving force. Psychologist Marvin Zuckerman summarized sensation seeking as, "a personality trait defined by the search for experiences and feelings that are varied, novel, complex, and intense, and by the readiness to take physical, social, legal, and financial risks for the sake of such experiences." Driving an old car is certainly novel and intense, and typically involves physical (and sometimes financial) risk.

Nobody gets out of life alive, and there's a level of risk inherent with a life well-lived, so we take the danger into account every time we drive, and we do it anyway. There are so many things beyond your control that contribute to the danger of daily life. There's a non-zero chance you could meet your proverbial maker catching the plague or take a digger tripping on the stairs, but it's irrational to let that fear prevent you from ever going outside or participating in society. Throw caution to the wind and take the old car to work today.

Many old-car enthusiasts view themselves as uniquely non-conformist. It's easy to go sign a loan for whatever new car you want to drive, but it takes a cultured individual to learn the ins and outs of an old car, find the right example, fix it, and keep it alive. There's a sense of pride in piloting an old car. While the normie NPCs drive around in new Camrys, we're bopping to the grocery store in Triumph Spitfires or Shelby Mustangs . An often-overlooked facet of vintage ownership, however, is being part of the group.

Joining a car club or ownership group (or the web forums of internet days gone by) is an extension of the self, helping determine your identity. I am happy to admit that I was influenced, at least in part, to buy my 1976 Porsche 912E because I'd participated in 912 Registry events and found the people therein to be as lovely as their cars. I was already leaning toward buying the car when it came up, but was pushed over the edge because the 912 people I met seemed like the group of people with which I wanted to associate. I like old Mustangs because my dad likes old Mustangs.

raw_title: 2026 Audi Q3 And Toyota RAV4 PHEV Underperform In IIHS Updated Moderate Overlap Crash Test
title: 2026 Audi Q3 And Toyota RAV4 PHEV Underperform In IIHS Updated Moderate Overlap Crash Test
raw_summary: You may think that all modern cars offer unimpeachable protection for their occupants in the event of a crash, but there's more variance and nuance in modern crash safety than you might be aware of. The Insurance Institute for Highway Safety or IIHS , published its first crash test ratings 30-years ago , in the year I was born, 1995. In those early days, its tests were criticized by automakers for being too severe, and yet those same automakers ended up building safer cars that aced the same tests just a few years later. As the American automotive landscape continues to evolve, the IIHS has evolved its tests , too, with the introduction of updated tests, like the new whiplash prevention test , the updated moderate front overlap test, and the updated side impact crash test that the 2026 Cadillac CT5 recently failed spectacularly . The tests conducted by the IIHS are extremely specific and controlled scenarios, but they establish an objective baseline by which to measure many areas of crash protection. The updates in IIHS tests over the years have uncovered new areas of vulnerability in some cars , and the latest crop of cars tested produced some unexpected results and clear weak points, specifically from cars like the all-new Audi Q3 and Toyota RAV4 .

article_paragraphs: You may think that all modern cars offer unimpeachable protection for their occupants in the event of a crash, but there's more variance and nuance in modern crash safety than you might be aware of. The Insurance Institute for Highway Safety or IIHS , published its first crash test ratings 30-years ago , in the year I was born, 1995. In those early days, its tests were criticized by automakers for being too severe, and yet those same automakers ended up building safer cars that aced the same tests just a few years later.

As the American automotive landscape continues to evolve, the IIHS has evolved its tests , too, with the introduction of updated tests, like the new whiplash prevention test , the updated moderate front overlap test, and the updated side impact crash test that the 2026 Cadillac CT5 recently failed spectacularly . The tests conducted by the IIHS are extremely specific and controlled scenarios, but they establish an objective baseline by which to measure many areas of crash protection. The updates in IIHS tests over the years have uncovered new areas of vulnerability in some cars , and the latest crop of cars tested produced some unexpected results and clear weak points, specifically from cars like the all-new Audi Q3 and Toyota RAV4 .

Let's start with the ever-popular Toyota RAV4. The IIHS just released results from the updated moderate overlap crash test for the redesigned 2026 Toyota RAV4 and RAV4 Plug-In Hybrid , and neither one earned the highest rating of Good. The RAV4 Hybrid earned the second-highest score of Acceptable, and the RAV4 PHEV earned the second-lowest score of Marginal in this test. Though these two cars are very similar, their different powertrains affect their performance in a variety of ways, including the PHEV's increased curb weight.

These less-than-perfect ratings are based on the way that the RAV4 protects the rear-seat passenger. In the regular RAV4 Hybrid, which earned the second-highest score of Acceptable, the rear passenger dummy recorded injury values that indicate a moderate risk of injury to the head or neck and chest, because the shoulder belt moved too far up toward the dummy's neck, compromising its effectiveness. It earned Acceptable ratings for rear passenger head and neck injuries, chest injuries, and the performance of its rear restraints.

The Marginal-rated RAV4 PHEV faced similar challenges with the performance of the rear-seat restraint system since its shoulder belt also moved toward the dummy's neck, but the lap belt also moved from its ideal position on the pelvis, up onto the abdomen, which increases the risk of abdominal injuries. The latter issue is a common reason why many new cars don't perform well in the updated moderate overlap crash test. When the lap belt remains in its ideal position on the big bony pelvis, it safely restrains the occupant without risking organ damage, but when the lap belt slips and cuts into the unprotected, organ-filled abdomen, it naturally poses additional injury risk.

The also-new Audi Q3 scored the IIHS lowest rating of Poor in the updated moderate overlap crash test for similar reasons to the RAV4. The Q3's biggest points of concern were a moderate risk of rear-seat occupant chest injury due to the shoulder belt slipping up toward the dummy's neck, and a Poor rating for the rear passenger restraints and dummy kinematics. The rear lap belt also moved from its ideal position securing the dummy's pelvis to the soft and vulnerable abdomen. It received Good ratings for its protection of the dummy's thighs as well as its head and neck, though.

The latest crop of updated moderate overlap test results also includes the 2026 and 2027 Nissan Kicks, 2026 Chevrolet Trailblazer, and the 2027 Volkswagen Jetta. Both the Nissan Kicks and the 2027 Volkswagen Jetta earned the top score of Good in the updated moderate overlap front crash test, but the 2026 Trailblazer earned the lowest rating of Poor.

The IIHS subjects cars to a barrage of different evaluations, including the small overlap front crash test, the updated side impact test, and front crash prevention tests with both vehicle-to-vehicle and vehicle-to-pedestrian scenarios. The institute evaluates their headlights, seat belt reminders, and the ease-of-use of their LATCH child seat anchors. There's a lot to cover there, and standards are always getting tougher.

article_paragraphs: Lando Norris and Kimi Antonelli were near-inseparable in final practice for Formula 1's Mexican Grand Prix as Ferrari's pace faltered ahead of qualifying.
Friday pacesetter Charles Leclerc ultimately ended up third for Ferrari, but only at the end of the session following aborted attempts at his qualifying simulation on soft tyres.
He and team-mate Lewis Hamilton - whose session played out in a similar way - had traded fastest times at the beginning of FP3 as the top teams all chose to start the session on medium tyres.

Mercedes was among the first of the frontrunners to switch to softs and while George Russell pondered whether a double-prep lap was necessary, telling the team to consider telling Antonelli to push after a single warm-up lap, Antonelli did complete two prep laps and duly went fastest with a 1m17.601s.
That looked as though it would stand as the session's best time until Norris improved with two minutes left of the hour-long session, going one thousandth quicker for McLaren.

Leclerc was 0.117s back in third, suggesting the Ferrari will remain a contender for pole in qualifying, while Oscar Piastri ended the session within two tenths of his pacesetting McLaren team-mate in fourth.

Max Verstappen complained of brake issues late on and was three and a half tenths down in fifth ahead of Hamilton, with less than seven hundredths covering the Ferrari in sixth and Arvid Lindblad at the back of the top 10, as Racing Bulls again had both drivers inside the theoretical Q3 cutoff.

Lindblad and ninth-fastest Lawson were well clear of their midfield rivals, with Nico Hulkenberg four tenths further back for Audi ahead of Alpine duo Franco Colapinto and Pierre Gasly and Fernando Alonso's Aston Martin.

title: Record Demand Catches (Some) OEMs with Their Pants Down
raw_summary: BEVs remain in high demand in Europe, with pure electrics reaching a record 31% share last month thanks to a record 422,000 fully electric passenger cars being registered in Europe, which is not only a 63%(!) increase year over year (YoY), but is also the fastest growth rate in over three years! Overall, plugin vehicles were up 49% YoY, dragged down by plugin hybrids, which grew only 23%, to 167,000 units, which was also a new record high for plugin hybrids in Europe, thus placing September’s total plugin volume at a best ever 590,000 units and its share at 43% (31% for BEVs only).

article_paragraphs: BEVs remain in high demand in Europe, with pure electrics reaching a record 31% share last month thanks to a record 422,000 fully electric passenger cars being registered in Europe, which is not only a 63%(!) increase year over year (YoY), but is also the fastest growth rate in over three years!

Overall, plugin vehicles were up 49% YoY, dragged down by plugin hybrids, which grew only 23%, to 167,000 units, which was also a new record high for plugin hybrids in Europe, thus placing September’s total plugin volume at a best ever 590,000 units and its share at 43% (31% for BEVs only).

With BEVs pulling the market upwards, the year-to-date share for BEVs is now at 25% (36% for PHEVs and BEVs combined) , which is already higher than the 2025 final result (20% BEV share, 29% adding PHEVs). This is an encouraging sign if we want to be close to 100% PEV share by the mid-2030s.

Looking at other powertrains, while petrol (18% share in September, down 21% YoY) and diesel (4%, down 28% YoY) continue their downward trend into irrelevance, the main news is the fact that we could have already passed the point of peak HEV — in September, plugless hybrids still grew, albeit less (+5% YoY) than the overall market (+10%, to 1.4 million units).

More important than that, if we compare the 34% share earned by HEVs in September 2026 with the share they had 12 months ago (36% then), we might be witnessing the beginning of plugless hybrids’ downward slope. So … if 2026 is the year of peak HEVs , how far are we from peak PHEVs ?
Looking at the best sellers in several size categories , the EV push is starting to get visible. While we are far from the EV domination we see in China, things are indeed evolving in Europe.

Before, the only EVs that we saw on the overall podiums were Teslas. Now, besides those two usual suspects , the 3rd placed model in the midsize category, the Mercedes GLC, is also heavily electrified, with 59% of all its sales coming from either its new BEV model (representing 44% of its total sales) or the PHEV versions (15% of sales), leaving the ICE versions representing just 41% of total sales.

The A-segment has the Renault Twingo as the 2nd placed model. Like in China before, expect this category to be quickly electrified. Firstly, the ICE competition is shrinking. Secondly, not only do we have the Renault Twingo already on the podium, but the new Dacia Spring is set to become a success, so expect it to join the Renault sibling on the podium. As a third musketeer, the VW ID.Up is set to land sometime next year, which is another strong bet from the German brand — and nothing shorter than a podium position would do.

summary: Unless you've been living under a rock, you've probably heard all the chatter about small trucks making a comeback. As you may already know, the compact Maverick has been a runaway success for Ford , and there's a lot of buzz surrounding the upcoming Fathom pickup.
article_paragraphs: Unless you've been living under a rock, you've probably heard all the chatter about small trucks making a comeback. As you may already know, the compact Maverick has been a runaway success for Ford , and there's a lot of buzz surrounding the upcoming Fathom pickup. Meanwhile, Slate Auto is expected to begin deliveries of its small truck by the end of 2026, Ram is readying a Maverick-sized competitor due to hit U.S. shores by 2030, and Kia has promised a midsize body-on-frame pickup by the end of the decade.

Although it feels as if automakers have found a groundbreaking formula and every brand is trying to capitalize on it, the idea is not new at all. In fact, Datsun brought the first compact truck to the U.S. in 1959 . Much of the '70s actually saw such pickups thrive. Why? They were honest work trucks — small, affordable, and practical, with reasonable utility.

Leading the charge were Toyota and Datsun, with their respective models enjoying strong sales. But it wasn't just Japanese brands, mind you. Domestic (albeit rebadged) offerings like the Chevy LUV, Ford Courier, and Plymouth Arrow were also part of the '70s compact-truck scene. In 1979 alone, Chevy managed to shift over 100,000 units of the LUV truck, which was essentially an Isuzu underneath.

While the small-truck trend continued into the '80s, GM and Ford developed their own models instead of badge-engineering Isuzu and Mazda trucks. Thus came the Chevy S-10 in 1982 and the Ford Ranger a year later. These trucks eventually grew in size with every redesign, and fast-forward to today, things are at a point where a top-spec Ford Ranger (now a midsize truck) costs north of $60,000. Size-wise, the current Ford Ranger is about an inch longer than a 2026 Mercedes-Benz S-Class.

Since modern pickup trucks have largely transitioned from their utilitarian roots to city-dwelling behemoths, it's easy to see why compact trucks like the Maverick are so successful. Not everyone has a huge F-150-sized hole in their life. Some people may still want a truck but don't want to put up with a full-sizer's massive dimensions or its gas-guzzling temperament.

The Maverick, for example, offers reasonable utility (up to 1,500 pounds of payload and a maximum towing capacity of 4,000 pounds), is fairly affordable (starting below $30,000), and has the safety tech and creature comforts that you'd expect in a modern automobile at that price point. Front-wheel-drive hybrids can also manage up to an EPA -estimated 42 mpg in the city.

The size argument, however, is a bit overblown. The "compact" Maverick, as it turns out, isn't that compact after all — it's over two inches longer than a midsize Land Rover Defender 110. The Slate Truck, on the other hand, is two feet shorter than the Maverick and has a longer bed. Think of it as a single-cab Maverick, if Ford ever offered one.

But if you find the Slate's electric-only propulsion a bit discouraging, there's the REO Runabout T4X that might be worth waiting for. Although it's still not production-ready, the truck is expected to be around 180 inches long (roughly half a foot longer than the Slate Truck) and feature a four-cylinder engine, four-wheel drive, and a towing capacity of 4,500 pounds, all while starting at $21,500.

article_paragraphs: US Federal Election Commission data revealed this week that Elon Musk has donated at least $445 million into Republican-aligned political action committees and groups since last year. Interestingly, it seems that Musk’s deep influence isn’t enough, and he is worried.
If Democrats win big on Tuesday in midterm elections, Musk insists US democracy will come to an “end.”

“This would result in America becoming a permanent one-party state and the end of democracy in any meaningful sense of the word,” Musk wrote Friday on X. “All that is needed to ensure this doesn’t happen is 51 Republican senators in 2029.”

The Tesla and SpaceX CEO has a long track record of engaging in political quid pro quo. His companies receive billions in federal contracts. The once climate-is-all advocate now weighs heavily on the side of oil/fossil fuels. His DOGE actions may have forced labor shortages in regulatory agencies that were scrutinizing his businesses.
But now Musk seems distraught that newfound Democratic Congressional power could make him a target of investigations after the midterms.
And his fears may have merit. Musk’s blatant attempts to influence election results are getting a lot of recent analysis and condemnation.

“I worry about what Musk’s impulsive bullying is doing and has done to others more vulnerable than I am,” former Secretary of Labor Robert Reich wrote earlier this month after Musk exclaimed, “Prison for Reich.” Such extreme comments are part of Musk lifelong pattern, Reich continued, in which “he’s threatened and racially denigrated and pushed around (people) his whole life.”

Reich added that he is worried for that voters whom Musk has been “deluging with TV ads for Republican candidates” as well as for “federal workers who have been hurt by his so-called Department of Government Efficiency, Americans who have been harmed by his wanton destruction of public services, and people around the globe who are worse off because of cuts to USAID pushed by Elon’s DOGE.”

raw_title: The Karma Eximius 1 Is a One-Off Hybrid Packing a 6.2-Liter V-8
title: The Karma Eximius 1 Is a One-Off Hybrid Packing a 6.2-Liter V-8
raw_summary: Personalization is the latest trend to sweep the automotive world, with nearly every high-end automaker launching a specific division that caters to the needs of its wealthiest customers. Porsche has Sonderwunsch, Bugatti has Sur Mesure, and Rolls-Royce has its Coachbuild program. Now Karma Automotive, a small American brand known for slinky plug-in hybrid sedans, is launching its own program called Eximius, and has revealed its first one-off, the Eximius 1, at the Concours at Wynn in Las Vegas. Karma Automotive, if you aren’t familiar, was birthed from the ashes of Fisker Automotive, and has sold an evolution of the Fisker Karma, known as the Revero and GS-6, on and off for most of the past decade. The Revero is a series hybrid, with a turbocharged three-cylinder serving as a generator to charge a battery that feeds electricity to a pair of rear-mounted electric motors. Although the Revero is being replaced by the new Gyesera, which further hones the same design and powertrain philosophy, this year, Karma is making sure the Revero goes out with a bang with this new one-off.

raw_title: The Essential Elements Of An Accurate 'Eleanor' Mustang Shelby Tribute
title: How To Build A Pure 'Eleanor' Mustang Shelby Replica: Complete Guide
raw_summary: The Eleanor Mustang from the 2000 remake of "Gone in 60 Seconds" hit the Mustang community like a bomb. The Steve Stanford design, adapted for production by Chip Foose, was a futuristic (for the time) take on the 1967 Shelby GT500. The silver-screen Shelby driven by Nic Cage inspired many replicas, and despite the film being more than a quarter of a century old, people are still obsessed with the thing. No fewer than four Eleanors crossed the block at last month's Barret-Jackson auction in Las Vegas. Despite the car's popularity, the history of Eleanor replicas is sordid. Denice Halicki, widow of the director of the 1974 original and rights holder of the "Gone in 60 Seconds" franchise, was infamously litigious. Any builder creating an Eleanor without a license could be hit with a copyright violation suit. Even YouTubers building replica Eleanors were not immune from Halicki's legal ire. But now, thanks to a 2025 federal court decision , Eleanor is legally considered a prop instead of a copyrightable character. You can make a visual replica — replete with a Leno-chinned body kit, enough auxiliary lights to make a WRC car blush, and a silver-with-black-stripes paint job — without getting sued into oblivion. Just don't officially call it an Eleanor, as the name is still trademarked.

You can make a visual replica — replete with a Leno-chinned body kit, enough auxiliary lights to make a WRC car blush, and a silver-with-black-stripes paint job — without getting sued into oblivion. Just don't officially call it an Eleanor, as the name is still trademarked.

Building a faithful Eleanor replica is not for the faint of heart or light of wallet. Thankfully, you don't have to start with a real Shelby GT500. The production team didn't. The bad news is that a 1967 Mustang fastback in decent shape won't be cheap. According to Hagerty's valuation data, a car in good condition with the base 289-cubic-inch V8 will set you back around $30,000. And that's before any of the body work that transforms a standard Mustang into an Eleanor.

Recreating the Stanford-designed exterior is where most of the work lies. Luckily, reproduction fiberglass body kits are readily available from suppliers like MustangBodyKit . Any complete kit should come with the Eleanor-specific parts, like bumpers, a hood, and fender flares, as well as GT500-style trunk extensions and a rear panel that allows for the fitment of 1967 or 1968 Mercury Cougar taillights. Just be aware that any fiberglass parts will need to be trimmed, fitted, and sanded before the car is painted. The correct colors come from Dupont's fleet catalog — Pepper Gray Metallic 44490 for the body and Black Metallic 44435 for the stripes.

With any Eleanor replica, the details matter. The production team switched up the location of the GT500 badges, using a pair of rear GT500 badges on the front fenders and a fender badge on the rear. The elliptical, side-exit exhaust tips can be purchased from suppliers like Mustangs to Fear . Rounding out the exterior details are 17-inch-by-8-inch Shelby Cobra-style wheels, Shelby-style bullet mirrors, a 1971-to-1973 Mach-1 flip-up gas cap, and PIAA driving lights up front. Note that the correct lights are no longer in production, so you'll need to find used versions or source alternatives.

After your wallet has been sufficiently lightened by all of the exterior changes, recreating the interior of an Eleanor may feel like a reprieve, because it's mostly mostly standard Mustang stuff. The movie cars started with the upscale Deluxe interior, which includes stainless-steel-trimmed bucket seats and aluminum accents on the dash and door panels. From there, a Lecarra wooden steering wheel was added, along with a ginormous AutoMeter Sport-Comp tach, Total Control Products aluminum pedal covers, a fire extinguisher mounted to the transmission tunnel, and, of course, a Hurst shifter with a Go Baby Go button to activate the nitrous bottle in the trunk.

Under the hood, most of the movie cars had a small-block Ford V8. For example, one of the surviving screen-used cars is equipped with a 351-cubic-inch Ford V8. But there was one 390 big-block car built for the L.A. River chase scene. Licensed Eleanor builders offer fuel-injected 427s and modern 5.0-liter Coyote engines. Even though the LS-series engines are popular for swaps for a reason , please resist the urge to put a Chevy V8 in there. As long as your Eleanor has a Ford V8 under the hood, the replica purity police shouldn't come after you. If you are still undeterred after reading all that goes into an Eleanor replica, go forth and build one. Just send us pics when you are done.

raw_summary: Isack Hadjar has been given a formal warning for pushing a guest in the paddock ahead of the first Formula 1 practice session at the Mexican Grand Prix. Footage circulated on social media on Friday that appeared to show Hadjar pushing someone who had tried to take a selfie with him.
