article_paragraphs: Isack Hadjar has been given a formal warning for pushing a guest in the paddock ahead of the first Formula 1 practice session at the Mexican Grand Prix.
Footage circulated on social media on Friday that appeared to show Hadjar pushing someone who had tried to take a selfie with him.
The Red Bull driver was subsequently called to see the F1 stewards on Saturday morning for what the summons document described as 'alleged misconduct'.

Hadjar stated in his appearance in front of the stewards that he was running late for FP1 and, having stopped for a photograph with a young fan, was "approached by a paddock guest in an aggressive manner".

The stewards' document detailing that account also said "one security person was walking behind him [Hadjar] and was unable to intervene and prevent what was tantamount to an invasion of the driver's private space".
Having initially resisted that move, Hadjar subsequently "pushed him aside with his open right hand" - a breach of article 12.2.1.l of the FIA international sporting code relating to misconduct.
However, in awarding only a warning the stewards acknowledge five mitigating circumstances in Hadjar's favour, in line with the guidelines in appendix B of the ISC.

These were that Hadjar was "reacting to an uninvited and rather aggressive action by another person"; that he was trying to make his way to the Red Bull garage for FP1 through a congested area; that he did not have "sufficient" security present; that the guest invaded his personal space without consent; and the "general issue" drivers have moving through the paddock.

summary: Katoen Natie has put two all-electric mobile harbour cranes into service at the Port of Antwerp, with four more joining them across three deep-sea multipurpose terminals. The completed fleet will include four 200-tonne cranes and two 150-tonne machines, with paired lifting capacity reaching 400 tonnes.
article_paragraphs: Katoen Natie has put two all-electric mobile harbour cranes into service at the Port of Antwerp, with four more joining them across three deep-sea multipurpose terminals. The completed fleet will include four 200-tonne cranes and two 150-tonne machines, with paired lifting capacity reaching 400 tonnes. Katoen Natie expects the six cranes to displace as much as 500,000 litres of diesel annually once they’re operating.

The October commissioning announcement is worth attention because these are heavy, mobile machines working in a commercial port. They aren’t small demonstrations, and the engineering addresses the conditions that historically made mobile harbour cranes difficult to electrify.

Fixed container cranes were straightforward candidates for electrification. They stay in one location, have repetitive operating patterns and can be connected to substantial electrical supplies. Mobile harbour cranes travel along the quay, move between assignments and handle cargo that can vary considerably from one vessel to the next. An onboard diesel generator provided that mobility without requiring the terminal to build electrical connections everywhere the crane might work.

Konecranes’ solution separates the energy needed for lifting from the energy needed for travel. External grid electricity supplies the heavy working loads, while rechargeable batteries allow the cranes to move between operating positions. This avoids carrying an enormous battery for work that can be powered directly from the grid. It also eliminates diesel exhaust at the equipment and reduces local noise.

The bigger advantage is that the investment isn’t tied to one type of cargo. A mobile harbour crane can handle steel, industrial equipment, large transformers, wind components, scrap, project cargo, conventional bulk and containers. Port operators can change their handling arrangements as customers and cargo flows change without replacing the basic lifting machinery.

That matters as the energy transition changes maritime trade. In an earlier CleanTechnica analysis , I examined how ports face rising capital requirements even as fossil-fuel cargoes begin their long-term decline. Coal, oil and gas have supported major investments in berths, terminals, channels and inland connections. Their declining role creates commercial risks for infrastructure designed around individual commodities.

Ports are looking for new business in containers, renewable-energy equipment, industrial products and alternative fuels. Some will succeed, but they cannot all capture the same growth in container traffic, and low-carbon molecules will not replace fossil-fuel cargo tonne for tonne. Equipment investments have to make sense under more than one plausible freight forecast.

Electric mobile cranes are well suited to that uncertainty. A machine capable of lifting a transformer today can handle scrap steel or construction machinery tomorrow. Its electrical supply can also be part of a wider investment supporting yard equipment, trucks, shore power and harbour craft.

title: How To Charge Your Car Battery Without Unhooking The Terminals
raw_summary: Few things are more annoying than trying to start your car and finding the battery is dead . Usually, this happens if you haven't driven for several weeks or months and the battery has slowly drained. Or, perhaps the battery has simply reached the end of its life. If it's the former, you generally won't need to rush out and buy a new battery. Instead, it's possible to charge a car's battery without unhooking the terminals, removing it from the car, or having to enlist a mechanic . There are many different car chargers on the market, ranging from less than $50 to more than $200. They work as you'd expect, slowly charging the battery over several hours. However, you need to follow a few key steps to charge a car battery safely.
summary: Few things are more annoying than trying to start your car and finding the battery is dead . Usually, this happens if you haven't driven for several weeks or months and the battery has slowly drained. Or, perhaps the battery has simply reached the end of its life.
article_paragraphs: Few things are more annoying than trying to start your car and finding the battery is dead . Usually, this happens if you haven't driven for several weeks or months and the battery has slowly drained. Or, perhaps the battery has simply reached the end of its life. If it's the former, you generally won't need to rush out and buy a new battery. Instead, it's possible to charge a car's battery without unhooking the terminals, removing it from the car, or having to enlist a mechanic .

There are many different car chargers on the market, ranging from less than $50 to more than $200. They work as you'd expect, slowly charging the battery over several hours. However, you need to follow a few key steps to charge a car battery safely.

First and foremost, pop the hood and find your car's battery. In most older vehicles, the battery sits on one side of the engine and is easy to spot. In newer cars, it may be hidden beneath a plastic cover you'll need to remove. In some cases, there might not be a battery in the engine bay, as with the Alfa Romeo Giulia Quadrifoglio we drove , which has its battery in the trunk.

Once you've found the battery, plug in the charger and ensure it's turned off. Next, attach the red lead to the battery's positive terminal and clamp the black cable to the negative terminal. On a battery that's completely drained, it's generally safe to attach the negative lead directly to the terminal. However, there is a safer way to do it.

In almost all modern vehicles, the negative battery terminal connects directly to the car's chassis. This means manufacturers don't need to run individual return wires for every part back to the battery. Instead, the vehicle's frame doubles as a shared return wire, reducing wiring complexity and weight. This means you can charge a car's battery by connecting the black lead to the chassis, since connecting it directly to the negative terminal can trigger a spark and an explosion, though that's unlikely.

Once everything is connected, just turn on the battery charger and wait for the magic to happen, while following the manufacturer's instructions. If you're in a rush and have a dead battery, a portable jump-start pack is another option. Though generally more expensive, these packs deliver enough power to start a vehicle without waiting around. Alternatively, car owners who don't drive their vehicles frequently can invest in a trickle charger.

I did just that the other week, buying a Noco Genius 2X2 that doubles as a battery charger and a trickle charger, which can maintain two car batteries at once. If you have a car that doesn't get driven frequently, a trickle charger is a great idea, as it keeps the battery fully topped up and ready to go. Advanced trickle chargers can be left plugged in and connected to a battery indefinitely, monitoring the battery's natural discharge rate and adding charge as required.

title: These 8 Modern Pony Cars Deliver Supercar Performance
raw_summary: It is not easy to define some automobile categories. What's the difference between a pony car and a muscle car? When does a sports car become a supercar, and when does the supercar become a hypercar? There are guidelines but also plenty of gray areas left up to interpretation. It is a bit like when Supreme Court Justice Potter Stewart tried to define obscenity by using the phrase "I know it when I see it." We are not here to attempt to come up with indisputable definitions for the pony car and the supercar. That would be futile and just lead to arguments. Instead, we decided to simply go with the most widely accepted definition of those types of automobiles.

article_paragraphs: It is not easy to define some automobile categories. What's the difference between a pony car and a muscle car? When does a sports car become a supercar, and when does the supercar become a hypercar? There are guidelines but also plenty of gray areas left up to interpretation. It is a bit like when Supreme Court Justice Potter Stewart tried to define obscenity by using the phrase "I know it when I see it."

We are not here to attempt to come up with indisputable definitions for the pony car and the supercar. That would be futile and just lead to arguments. Instead, we decided to simply go with the most widely accepted definition of those types of automobiles.

The Ford Mustang is generally credited with ushering in the pony car era. The pony car category even gets its name thanks to the Mustang. It is an American car with a long hood, short deck, a stylish design, and sporty performance.

Speaking of supercars, the Lamborghini Miura is generally accepted as the original. When it was revealed at the Geneva Motor Show on March 10, 1966, it introduced to the world a whole new class of automobile for the street. The V12 engine is mounted transversely behind the driver. It has an intoxicating design, and with a top speed of 163 mph, it was the world's fastest production car.

Historically, a supercar carried a higher price but offered greater performance in exchange. The price gap is still there, but the performance gap has narrowed dramatically in recent years. The Camaro Z/28, Challenger SRT Demon 170, and Shelby GT350R are all capable of supercar-humbling performance. And they are not alone. Here's a closer look at eight pony cars that can keep supercar owners up at night.

A fifth-generation Camaro Z/28 isn't going to grab the attention of bystanders the same way a Ferrari F12 will. In fact, most people on the street probably could not even tell the difference between a 2015 Z/28 and a rental car-spec Camaro LS. But that somewhat pedestrian-looking Camaro Z/28 will run nearly neck and neck around Virginia International Raceway's 4.1-mile Grand Course with the V12 Ferrari.

That is because lurking under the hood is the same LS7 V8 engine that is found in the C6 Corvette Z06. That means that you can control 505 horsepower with your right foot. But perhaps even more impressive than the raw power are the components that GM engineers added to make the car a legitimate track weapon. Remember, the original 1967 Z/28 was developed to compete in the SCCA's Trans-Am series. The Z/28 has a reputation to protect.

One way to protect it was to install Mulitmatic-developed dynamic suspension spool valve (DSSV) dampers. That suspension combined with sticky Pirelli PZero Trofeo R tires give this car incredible grip and control. Combine that with the LS7 power and you have a $76,000 Camaro that can lap a racetrack as quickly as a $320,000 Ferrari. The Camaro Z/28 may be a pony car, but it has supercar performance.

title: The Secret Engineering Behind Why The Lexus IS F And RC F 2UR-GSE V8 Never Dies
raw_summary: Every gearhead knows reliability is unlikely to be a sore spot when you're dealing with a Lexus. A good chunk of that reputation is understandably tied to its engines, which regularly pass 200,000 miles with nothing more than routine maintenance. However, the same sentiment also extends to the brand's high-performance engines, like the tantalizing 2UR-GSE, a 5.0-liter 32-valve DOHC V8 found in Lexus' now-discontinued performance models like the IS F, RC F, GS F, and ultimate continent-crossing grand touring LC 500 . The 2UR-GSE V8 made its debut for the 2008 model year in the Lexus IS F, designed to challenge BMW M, Mercedes-AMG, and Audi S performance cars at their own game. To ensure it brought durability along with it, the engineers combined a strong bottom end with a naturally aspirated design, eliminating the additional heat and stress caused by forced induction.
summary: Every gearhead knows reliability is unlikely to be a sore spot when you're dealing with a Lexus. A good chunk of that reputation is understandably tied to its engines, which regularly pass 200,000 miles with nothing more than routine maintenance.
article_paragraphs: Every gearhead knows reliability is unlikely to be a sore spot when you're dealing with a Lexus. A good chunk of that reputation is understandably tied to its engines, which regularly pass 200,000 miles with nothing more than routine maintenance. However, the same sentiment also extends to the brand's high-performance engines, like the tantalizing 2UR-GSE, a 5.0-liter 32-valve DOHC V8 found in Lexus' now-discontinued performance models like the IS F, RC F, GS F, and ultimate continent-crossing grand touring LC 500 .

The 2UR-GSE V8 made its debut for the 2008 model year in the Lexus IS F, designed to challenge BMW M, Mercedes-AMG, and Audi S performance cars at their own game. To ensure it brought durability along with it, the engineers combined a strong bottom end with a naturally aspirated design, eliminating the additional heat and stress caused by forced induction.

The 2UR-GSE was built using a die-cast aluminum alloy block featuring five main bearings for the forged crankshaft, with each main bearing cap secured by a rare six-bolt design typically reserved for full-on race engines, adding structural rigidity under high loads and high revs. Like most reliable engines, instead of timing belts, it uses timing chains that typically last the entire lifetime of the engine.

But even so, the 2UR-GSE V8 has a conservative redline of between 6,800 and 7,300 rpm, giving it plenty of headroom to operate reliably. Meanwhile, up top, the aluminum cylinder head was sealed to the engine block with a head gasket constructed from three layers of steel laminate with each gasket including a shim around the cylinder bore to strengthen the seal. Inside, lightweight titanium valves help keep revs high.

The 2UR-GSE V8's design does more than just make it reliable. It also helps it produce serious power without compromising on durability. A blend of its Yamaha-designed, high-flow cylinder head, high compression ratio (initially 11.8:1), dual variable valve timing (VVT-i), and Toyota's D-4S direct and port injection system allows early versions of the 2UR-GSE to produce 416 horsepower and 371 pound-feet of torque in the IS F. Then, following the arrival of the RC F in 2014, power output rose to 467 hp and 389 lb-ft, thanks to a combination of a bigger throttle body (the diameter was stepped up in size from 76mm to 83mm), a revised intake valve with more lift that stays open for longer, as well as redesigned intake ports that move more air through the engine. Lexus also bumped the compression ratio up to 12.3:1.

Fast forward half a decade, and engineers went about uprating the powertrain yet again as part of the sport car's midlife facelift for the 2020 model year, with output rising by 5 hp and 6 lb-ft to 472 hp and 395 lb-ft in total, achieved through better intake routing — enough to make the 2UR-GSE the most powerful V8 engine Lexus ever made .

Sadly, this version of the engine never went into the original IS F sedan, as it was taken off sale right before even the 467-hp variant of the engine launched for the 2015 model year. Instead, if you're set on a Lexus sports sedan, the Lexus IS 500 F Sport Performance also comes with the same 472-hp version of the 2UR-GSE V8.

While the 2UR-GSE has garnered a reputation for being nearly indestructible, there are still some things to watch out for when buying a used Lexus with this V8 engine. Many expert sources report that problems with the valley plate can occur. For instance, the factory sealant used to bond the valley plate to the engine block can degrade and fail due to repeated heat cycles — although some attribute the issue to the Lexus pink "super long-life coolant". This could lead to coolant leaks and heighten the risk of the engine overheating and ultimately failing. Any issues with the sealant around the valley plate will typically manifest as a puddle of pink coolant under the intake manifold.

title: Inside A Police Cruiser: What Officers Actually Carry In The Trunk
raw_summary: There's a lot that separates police cars from other vehicles , but have you ever wondered what cops keep in the back of their cruisers? Surely, they use that space for something, extra sandwiches and other snacks, maybe? Well, according to our research, it turns out there is a wide variety of practical gear stored in a squad car's trunk, everything from safety equipment to riot gear. However, sandwiches weren't listed in any of the sources we could find, sadly. Of course, which kind of practical gear is stored depends on which police department the officer is a part of and what they do within that department. A highway patrol officer, for example, may carry items for controlling traffic around an accident, like cones and flares, along with crash investigation kits. An officer in an urban area who is often called to disturbances may carry more tactical gear, like bulletproof vests and helmets. Officers who are often called to crime scenes may carry things like crime scene tape and evidence collection bags. Most police cars will also have gear to help in medical emergencies.

article_paragraphs: There's a lot that separates police cars from other vehicles , but have you ever wondered what cops keep in the back of their cruisers? Surely, they use that space for something, extra sandwiches and other snacks, maybe? Well, according to our research, it turns out there is a wide variety of practical gear stored in a squad car's trunk, everything from safety equipment to riot gear. However, sandwiches weren't listed in any of the sources we could find, sadly.

Of course, which kind of practical gear is stored depends on which police department the officer is a part of and what they do within that department. A highway patrol officer, for example, may carry items for controlling traffic around an accident, like cones and flares, along with crash investigation kits. An officer in an urban area who is often called to disturbances may carry more tactical gear, like bulletproof vests and helmets. Officers who are often called to crime scenes may carry things like crime scene tape and evidence collection bags. Most police cars will also have gear to help in medical emergencies.

Every department is different, obviously. Some nice person donated a whole bunch of homemade stuffed animals to the Franklin, Tennessee, police department. Many of the officers carry them in their vehicles to help calm children at a crime or accident scene. Teddy bears are not standard issue in most police departments around the country, obviously. It may be something they should consider, though.

Sometimes, cops are among the first responders at a scene. That means, depending on the emergency, the officer may have to double temporarily as a firefighter or paramedic. That's why many police cars have a fire extinguisher in the cargo area. Of course, these would only be useful for putting out small fires, as opposed to saving your six-bedroom McMansion that has been set ablaze.

As you can imagine, police generally carry plenty of medical items with them. This would include a fully-stocked first-aid kit, along with a trauma kit containing gear to control severe bleeding. Blankets are often included to keep injured or exposed people warm. Those are probably items we should all carry in our cars' emergency kits . There may also be entry and exit tools in case they have to force their way into a locked car or house. Many police departments issue their officers Narcan, or Naloxone, which is administered to people going through an opioid overdose. Blood-borne kits and hand disinfectant are also must-haves.

We were surprised to find out that many police cars have an AED, or automated external defibrillator, their cargo areas. These machines are used to monitor someone's heart rate and to give them a shock if that rate is too low. It's a good thing cops are trained to use defibrillators. After all, the police can't let McDonald's employees make them look bad.

You may expect there to be a bunch of tactical gear in the trunk of a cop car, and you'd be right. For example, stop sticks, which are specially designed to deflate tires without making them explode , are often stored in the trunks of police vehicles. Police cars may also carry a battering ram, a sledgehammer, bolt cutters, bulletproof helmets, riot gear, and bulletproof vests. There is also something called a "ballistic blanket." We didn't know what that was, so we had to look it up. It's exactly what it sounds like — a bulletproof blanket.

If an officer is assigned to process crime scenes, they will carry equipment such as crime scene tape, evidence bags, and other collection supplies. To help with accidents and other roadside events, a cop's trunk may also contain traffic cones, flares, and other traffic control equipment. In addition to all of the police stuff, cops need to have practical items like the rest of us carry in our trunks for car emergencies. Can you imagine how embarrassing it would be to have remembered to pack your ballistic blanket only to have left your jumper cables back at the precinct?

Surely, they use that space for something, extra sandwiches and other snacks, maybe?
Well, according to our research, it turns out there is a wide variety of practical gear stored in a squad car's trunk, everything from safety equipment to riot gear.

raw_title: 6 Of The Most Powerful Engines Ever Put In A Motorcycle
title: 6 Of The Most Powerful Engines Ever Put In A Motorcycle
raw_summary: Given the lightweight nature of motorcycles, many of them can get away with using small single-cylinder engines that don't make much power — the majority of everyday bikes and scooters use this type of engine. Meanwhile, experienced riders with enough cash lying around can opt for cruisers, tourers, and superbikes with multi-cylinder engines developing triple-digit horsepower figures. However, over the years, many enthusiasts, automakers, and boutique firms have pushed the limits of power in motorcycles to levels that defy belief. We're talking engines and power outputs that'd be considered impressive even by car standards, but are simply ludicrous in a motorcycle. Below, you'll find six of the most powerful engines ever fitted to a motorcycle — from V4s to a stonking V10 — with outputs ranging from 220 hp to over 600. We ranked them all from least to most powerful. It's quite an eclectic mix of motorcycles too, comprising production models that you can walk into a showroom and buy, track-only bikes that cost an arm and a leg, and one-off projects built by incredibly talented engineers.

If you're a fan of MotoGP, the Aprilia RSV4 Factory 1100 is possibly the closest you can get to a racing-bike experience while still being street-legal and relatively attainable. Nestled within the RSV4 Factory 1100's twin-spar aluminum frame is a 65-degree 1.1-liter V4 developing 220 hp at 13,000 rpm and 93.7 lb-ft of torque at 10,800 rpm, which is routed to the tarmac via a six-speed multi-plate wet-clutch gearbox.

While its engine is retained from the standard RSV4, the Factory 1100 adds a bunch of suspension and feature upgrades for better on-track performance. Specifically, it gets an Öhlins USD fork up front and an Öhlins monotube at the rear, both electronically controlled. It also comes with lighter forged alloy wheels, and additional features like launch control, GPS, a pit-speed limiter, slide control, and cruise control.

Thanks to its 450-pound wet weight, the RSV4 Factory 1100 carries an exceptional power-to-weight ratio of 0.49 hp-per-pound, allowing for a top speed of over 190 mph. And what do you pay for all this searing performance? Surprisingly, not that much, at least when compared to the other super-powerful motorcycles on this list. Aprilia has the RSV4 Factory 1100 listed at $26,749, excluding a $1,325 destination fee.

Unveiled earlier this year to commemorate Ducati's 100th anniversary, the Superleggera V4 Centenario immediately wowed everyone by becoming the Italian manufacturer's most powerful street-legal motorcycle yet. It achieves this thanks to a new engine, the Desmosedici Stradale R 1100, which is based on the Panigale V4 R's 1.0-liter V4. However, Ducati has increased the piston stroke, resulting in a slightly higher 1.1-liter displacement.

In its standard configuration, the Superleggera V4 Centenario produces 228 hp at 14,500 rpm and 86.7 lb-ft at 10,500 rpm, and if you opt for the Akrapovič racing exhaust and Ducati Corse Performance oil, that output rises to 247 hp at 14,750 rpm and 93.2 lb-ft at 12,500 rpm, channeled to the road via a six-speed racing gearbox. These figures not only make the Superleggera V4 Centenario the most powerful road-going Ducati, but also the most powerful street-legal naturally-aspirated superbike in the world. If you want one, however, you're out of luck. Ducati will build only 500 examples, each priced at $165,000 before options plus a $1,495 destination fee, and all of them are already spoken for.

Built purely for the racetrack1, the Kawasaki H2R is one of the fastest bikes in the world. It carries over the standard Kawasaki H2's 1.0-liter supercharged inline-4 engine, but with an uprated output of 322 hp at 14,000 rpm and 121.5 lb-ft of torque at 12,500 rpm. Kawasaki achieved this power bump by remapping the ECU along with installing more aggressive camshaft profiles, a stronger head gasket and clutch, an unrestricted carbon-fiber intake, and a super-loud titanium exhaust system.

title: Ocon suddenly replaced at Haas for rest of Mexico F1 weekend
raw_summary: Esteban Ocon will sit out the rest of Formula 1's Mexican Grand Prix with Haas reserve driver Ryo Hirakawa replacing him. Haas unexpectedly released a short statement on Saturday morning announcing the switch.
summary: Esteban Ocon will sit out the rest of Formula 1's Mexican Grand Prix with Haas reserve driver Ryo Hirakawa replacing him. Haas unexpectedly released a short statement on Saturday morning announcing the switch.
article_paragraphs: Esteban Ocon will sit out the rest of Formula 1's Mexican Grand Prix with Haas reserve driver Ryo Hirakawa replacing him.
Haas unexpectedly released a short statement on Saturday morning announcing the switch.
"TGR Haas F1 team reserve driver Ryo Hirakawa will replace Esteban Ocon for the remainder of the weekend's Mexico City Grand Prix," the statement read.

"Hirakawa, a two-time winner of the FIA World Endurance Championship and 24 Hours of Le Mans Winner with Toyota Gazoo Racing, participated in FP1 at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez on Friday 30 October - his third free practice outing of the season driving the VF-26, finishing 15th overall.
"The Japanese driver will partner team-mate Ollie Bearman through final practice and qualifying on Saturday and Sunday's 71-lap grand prix - Hirakawa's Formula 1 race debut.
No reason has been given for the change but Haas has confirmed it is not due to illness for Ocon.
It is logical therefore to reason that he appears to have been benched.

Ocon had a frustrating Friday in Mexico, publicly expressing his dissatisfaction with his runplan in FP2 - his only session in the car, after 32-year-old Hirakawa drove in FP1 to satisfy the rookie practice rule.

raw_title: How F1 teams are tackling Mexico's altitude challenge in 2026
title: How F1 teams are tackling Mexico's altitude challenge in 2026
raw_summary: The Mexico City track is one of the outliers of the Formula 1 season, mainly because of the altitude: it is 2240 meters above sea level, which equates to roughly 25% less dense air, so it makes everything just that bit more difficult. For the drivers it's basically harder work, but for the cars it's a very different story, because at that altitude the cars will produce less downforce and with that less drag. In the past, teams would use more or less Monaco-specification wings but this season with the change in wing regulations and active aero they don't have that possibility.

article_paragraphs: The Mexico City track is one of the outliers of the Formula 1 season, mainly because of the altitude: it is 2240 meters above sea level, which equates to roughly 25% less dense air, so it makes everything just that bit more difficult.

For the drivers it's basically harder work, but for the cars it's a very different story, because at that altitude the cars will produce less downforce and with that less drag. In the past, teams would use more or less Monaco-specification wings but this season with the change in wing regulations and active aero they don't have that possibility.

So, basically the ars will slide around more but the reduced drag means that top speeds are even faster than normal. This means that you will arrive at the end of those long straights faster and require a longer braking duration, which generates more heat in the brakes.

These cars are turbocharged so in reality even though the turbo has to work harder and will be running at or as near to its maximum rpm as possible for most of the lap, it will still produce similar levels of power output. This means the engine's heat rejection isn't reduced, so you need to cool the cars roughly 25% more than you normally have to.
Also, as it's an electrical energy-rich circuit layout you will also generate more heat into the battery pack and its control systems simply from harvesting and deployment.

Basically, everything needs higher levels of cooling and below I have had a look at the top-four teams' changes from what they normally run. It's not easy to alter the inlet area on these cars as it is part of the side impact structure, so changing it would basically require redoing the side impact tests, so instead everyone will focus on the cooling exits, size, location and quantity.
First of all we can have a look at the rear exits.
The red ellipse highlights the rearwards-facing outlet. McLaren has raised the section above the exhaust outlet to increase the exit area.

title: 7 Toyota Models That Hold Their Value Best After Five Years
raw_summary: Depreciation is a double-edged sword, but whether you're buying or selling, one brand consistently tops the list for the lowest depreciation over five years: Toyota. CarEdge reports that Toyota models, on average, retain 64.9% of their original value. Subaru, at 61.2%, comes in second. Think about that Toyota number for a moment. The average new car loses roughly 30% of its MSRP in the first two years of ownership. It takes a Toyota almost half a decade to do the same. But remember that value hit is an average; some Toyota models have even stronger residual values. At the top of Toyota's list for lowest depreciation are the Tacoma, Corolla Hatchback, GR Supra, 4Runner, Tundra, RAV4, and the regular Corolla sedan. Other models, like the Corolla Cross and Grand Highlander, also have below-average depreciation, but these nameplates haven't been around for very long. We're focusing on Toyotas with a five-year valuation track record that's been reported by CarEdge and iSeeCars, and the value retention percentage we highlighted for each model in this list averages the two companies' calculations.

The average new car loses roughly 30% of its MSRP in the first two years of ownership. It takes a Toyota almost half a decade to do the same. But remember that value hit is an average; some Toyota models have even stronger residual values.

At the top of Toyota's list for lowest depreciation are the Tacoma, Corolla Hatchback, GR Supra, 4Runner, Tundra, RAV4, and the regular Corolla sedan. Other models, like the Corolla Cross and Grand Highlander, also have below-average depreciation, but these nameplates haven't been around for very long. We're focusing on Toyotas with a five-year valuation track record that's been reported by CarEdge and iSeeCars, and the value retention percentage we highlighted for each model in this list averages the two companies' calculations.

To add a dose of reality, we also looked at active listings from Autotrader to see how closely those valuations hold up in today's marketplace. All MSRPs mentioned include factory destination charges. Used-vehicle pricing reflects examples with near-average mileage for their age (around 68,000 miles for a five-year-old vehicle) and in good condition with no accident history or branded titles.

While owners have different opinions about the best Toyota Tacoma generation , one thing is indisputable: A five-year-old Tacoma is the residual-value champion among similarly aged Toyotas. CarEdge says that works out to 79% of its original value after five years, while iSeeCars is more generous with 80.1%. That's a retained-value average of 79.5%. Or put another way, the Tacoma loses only about 4% of its value per year. iSeeCars also lists the Tacoma as one of the top vehicles for low depreciation — only the Porsche Cayman, Porsche 911, and Chevrolet Corvette are better.

A 2021 Tacoma in SR5 trim, with rear-wheel drive and a double cab, averages roughly $29,500 on Autotrader. When new, the MSRP for this version was $33,405. Crunch those numbers, and five-year depreciation only rises to 11.7%. The 88.3% residual value is substantially above the combined average from CarEdge and iSeeCars.

Although the GR Supra is leaving the Toyota lineup after 2026 , this BMW-built sports car is alive and well in the used car market. CarEdge's data shows a five-year residual value of 78.4%, while iSeeCars is close at 76%; the two estimates average 77.2%. The GR Supra launched for the 2020 model year, with the 2021 edition adding a lower-priced four-cylinder version alongside a more robust inline-6 model, which received a 47-horsepower bump.

Despite the four-cylinder's more affordable base price of $43,985, a 2021 GR Supra still costs more used than a new Toyota GR86. Marketplace pricing for this base model hovers around $37,000, putting its retained value at 84.1% — higher than the CarEdge and iSeeCars estimates. Adding a six-cylinder engine to the conversation increases valuations slightly. With limited inventory, the mid-grade 3.0 Premium trim, which had an original MSRP of $55,485, is listed at an average of $47,000 on Autotrader, which points to a resale value of 84.7%.

Toyota's full-size pickup, the Tundra, also makes the cut for keeping depreciation to a minimum. However, five-year resale value estimates of 75.5% ( CarEdge ) and 78.8% ( iSeeCars ) leave a 3.3-percentage-point gap between the two sources. That difference can translate into a $1,200-or-more price difference for used truck buyers. The 2021 model year is the last edition of the second generation, which was replaced by an all-new Toyota Tundra with the grenading V6 engine .

title: Renault And Peugeot Revived Group B Rally Legends As EVs, But Which Did It Better?
raw_summary: If you had told a Group B spectator back in the '80s that the spirit of the monstrous rally cars would be resurrected forty years later without a single drop of gasoline, they would have probably laughed. article_paragraphs: If you had told a Group B spectator back in the '80s that the spirit of the monstrous rally cars would be resurrected forty years later without a single drop of gasoline, they would have probably laughed. However, that's exactly what happened with two French unicorns from Renault and Peugeot, swapping their turbocharged engines for electric motors and battery packs.

We're talking about the spiritual successors of the mid-engine rear-wheel-drive Renault 5 Maxi Turbo and the all-wheel-drive Peugeot 205 T16, both envisioned as fully electric wide-bodied hyper hatchbacks. In order to see which did it best, we gathered photos and specs in an early comparison, well before anyone has had a chance to drive them back to back. First came the Renault Turbo 3E, with a retro-flavored concept study in 2022 evolving into a limited-production 535-hp supercar special in 2025. Meanwhile, the Peugeot e-T16 concept debuted in 2026, and could be heading to production in 2027.

While both models revive motorsport icons from the past, there is a fundamental difference in their design intentions. The Renault is a flagship performance EV that bridges the gap between the classic R5 Turbo and the new R5 E-Tech, while the Peugeot is a cleverly disguised hyper-aggressive preview of the 208 hatchback which is due in 2027 . Still, with both rally-inspired EVs targeting a similar niche, many collectors will be divided on which one will end up in their dream garage (if not both).

Starting with the exterior design, the R5 Turbo 3E looks like a modernized version of its legendary Group B descendant, with futuristic styling cues such as the fancy LEDs, advanced aerodynamics, and the 20-inch alloy wheels. On the other hand, the Peugeot e-T16 Group B rally homage leans into the modern era, although it carries the spirit of the 205 in its the characteristic greenhouse, red stripes, and boxy taillights. What's new is the three-slot full-width LED graphics on the headlights and the taillights, set to become a signature trait of future Peugeots.

It also rides on slightly larger 21-inch alloys with wider tires at the back. Both models stay true to the motorsport theme by adopting aggressive bumper intakes, prominent splitters, ultra-wide fenders with integrated vents, deep side skirts, sizeable rear diffusers and roof spoilers. Despite the fact that all production superminis now have five doors, the French hyper hatchbacks retain the traditional three-door layout that used to be the norm.

While automakers created the original Group B hatchbacks by ripping out the rear seats and placing a combustion engine behind the driver, their modern successors rely on clever EV packaging to replicate that mid-engined feel. The Renault uses a bespoke aluminum tubular chassis developed by Alpine, and a floor-mounted 70-kWh battery contributing to a 43/57 weight distribution. As with the original, the R5 Turbo 3E remains rear-wheel-drive.

Dual electric motors produce a combined 555 horsepower (410 kW/563 PS), allowing a 0-100 km/h (0-62 mph) sprint in under 3.5 seconds. The Renault is also the lighter of the pair, weighing 1,450 kg (3,197 lbs). The Peugeot utilizes Stellantis' new STLA One global architecture , but stays true to the all-wheel-drive nature of the 205 T16. Three electric motors produce a combined 816 hp (600 kW/827 PS), easily outgunning the Group B rally cars of the past.

Acceleration is even more impressive, launching from 0-100 km/h (0-62 mph) in 2.5 seconds. The battery has a capacity of 85 kWh and promises to have enough juice for three consecutive laps around the Nürburgring. While Peugeot hasn't published the exact curb weight, they state the e-T16 has a power-to-weight ratio of under 2 kg/hp (4.4 lbs/hp), hinting at a 1,632 kg (3,590 lbs) figure. As for charging, the Renault can go from 15-80% and the Peugeot from 10-80% in about 15 minutes as long as you have access to the right charger.

raw_title: What Will Transportation Look Like In The U.S. In 2050?
title: What Will Transportation Look Like In The U.S. In 2050?
raw_summary: Depending on who you ask, the motor car was brought to life in Europe, but it was Henry Ford that brought it to the masses from the U.S. By the Jet Age, technology had already advanced so quickly, humanity's dream was a place in the stars and with flying cars, reflected in jet-inspired, futuristic designs on everything from cars to toasters. We'd certainly be in flying cars by the 21st century, right? But we're 26 years into the 21st century and still flying on the same planes that revolutionized the skies almost 70 years ago. The technology operating those aircraft and vehicles is different, but the cars aren't flying. And thank goodness, because a good portion of the population can barely drive. Can you imagine them also flying? Humanity has been inching closer to that future, but there are still big hurdles to clear. We are clearly struggling through the growing pains of possible driverless technology , and no matter what Florida does when it comes to flying VTOLs and e-VTOLs , regular commuters won't have flying transport in their future any time soon.

The future feels a bit murky right now, too, as the gas crisis caused by the U.S. and Iran war has sent consumers towards adopting electric cars , all while the U.S. continues to eliminate fuel economy restrictions. With all the turmoil, what will transportation look like in the U.S. in the year 2050? That's what I want to know.

The romantic optimist in me dreams of a future where leaders come to their senses and realize investing money in public transportation (extended to rural areas) and high speed rails will improve accessibility and affordability for everyone. Can we really change that much in 24 years, though? After the last 10, it's difficult to say.

Here's how I see it: In the year 2050, if Detroit's automakers survive, they'll barely be hanging on. And to my mind, the biggest threat to the automotive scene is now Amazon. Obviously, by that point, it will have beaten out SpaceX-Tesla because Amazon already delivers anything the American people need at a moment's notice. With grocery delivery, drone delivery, and drivers that deliver seven days a week, why not also figure out a way to deliver people too? Jeff Bezos invested in the Slate truck and quickly brought it back into the fold as an Amazon Basics product.

Amazon's autonomous vehicles (because it has those too) will deliver you to your Amazon factory job, because we still won't have nailed down robots . Otherwise, people won't need to leave the house much because everything can be brought to your Amazon-made home. You won't need public transportation if you're at home all day, everyday, putting in time to help power the Amazon grid.

With that nightmare now out in the world, it's your turn to tell us what you think transportation will look like here in the U.S. in 2050. Maybe your vision is a bit more optimistic. Seeing as the biggest things we've gotten in the last 25 years are massive home offices on wheels, electric cars, and some hands-off driving, a realist might predict improvements in those sectors, and possibly the death of some auto companies. Let us know what you think in the comments below.

title: Can Silicon Valley Build A Safe Class 8 Truck? Early EV Semi Fires Expose The Experience Gap
raw_summary: If you drove through the East Bay area of California on Tuesday night, you probably got caught in a nightmare. A Tesla Semi traveling down Interstate 880 in Hayward caught fire during the evening commute. There was no crash, no multi-vehicle pileup, and no obvious collision. The driver noticed something was wrong, pulled over near Highway 92, and got out unharmed. Then the lithium-ion pack did what high-energy battery chemistry does when it gets pushed past its thermal limits… By the time crews finished foaming down the wreckage, all that remained of the tractor was its rear axles and a pile of ash.

article_paragraphs: If you drove through the East Bay area of California on Tuesday night, you probably got caught in a nightmare. A Tesla Semi traveling down Interstate 880 in Hayward caught fire during the evening commute. There was no crash, no multi-vehicle pileup, and no obvious collision. The driver noticed something was wrong, pulled over near Highway 92, and got out unharmed.

Then the lithium-ion pack did what high-energy battery chemistry does when it gets pushed past its thermal limits… By the time crews finished foaming down the wreckage, all that remained of the tractor was its rear axles and a pile of ash.

The California Highway Patrol shut down both directions of the freeway out of concern over toxic chemical smoke. Northbound lanes eventually opened back up, but southbound lanes stayed closed for nearly ten hours while fire crews managed the blaze and let the pack burn itself out. When the sun came up, all that remained of the tractor was its rear axles and a pile of ash.

This is the second time in just over two years that a single Tesla Semi has shut down a major California highway for half a day. Back in August 2024, a Tesla-operated Semi drifted off Interstate 80 near Emigrant Gap, hit a tree, and caught fire. It took 50,000 gallons of water, air drops from Cal Fire, and a 15-hour closure to clear the road.

Whenever this happens, the anti-EV crowd immediately pounces and claims electric trucks are rolling time bombs. That’s a lie, as we’ve repeatedly explained here, but the knee-jerk reaction from tech enthusiasts, which claims this is just normal trucking business, is equally disconnected from reality.

Something deeper is going on here, and it highlights an important cultural divide between Silicon Valley and the century-old world of heavy-duty commercial trucking. Instead of trashing people and pointing fingers, let’s look at a deeper lesson the industry can learn from this.

According to the National Fire Protection Association, US fire departments respond to roughly 15,000 large truck fires every single year. That is about 40 diesel rigs catching fire every day across the country. Blown turbochargers spray oil on hot exhaust manifolds, wheel-end bearings seize at 70 mph, and dragging drum brakes ignite recap tires. Diesel trucks burn all the time, so fire is not a phenomenon unique to electric trucks.

The difference is how they burn. When a diesel tractor catches fire, the local volunteer fire department can usually knock it down with an engine tank and some foam in 45 minutes. A heavy tow truck drags the scorched chassis off the road, sweepers clear the debris, and traffic starts moving again before the morning rush hour is ruined.

title: 9 Of The Most Popular Japanese Performance Cars To Import (And Why Enthusiasts Love Them)
raw_summary: A certain breed of American car enthusiast is very good at taking any year in the late 20th century and adding 25. It's like "Rain Man," but for extremely simple arithmetic. They're determining whether a vehicle sold abroad has reached 25 years old, thus exempting it from Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards in the U.S., and making it fair game for American import. It's the mechanism by which countless Skylines, Evo variants, and performance Hondas — not to mention the occasional kei car — have found their way stateside, and you really just need to know how to import a Japanese car to America without making your head explode if you want to pull it off yourself. Right now, that 25-year math is opening the door on a whole new batch of turn-of-the-millennium vehicles: What's up, Japanese Domestic Market Honda Integra Type R from 2001? But that 25-year window has been rolling for a while now, and some clear favorites have emerged. Japanese import marketplace JDMBuySell maintains a ranking of the most-watched JDM vehicles, combining buyer inquiries on its site with American Google search activity to gauge demand. Those aren't import totals, but they offer a pretty good indication of what enthusiasts are shopping for. Here are nine of the most popular choices, and why people want them.

Japanese import marketplace JDMBuySell maintains a ranking of the most-watched JDM vehicles, combining buyer inquiries on its site with American Google search activity to gauge demand. Those aren't import totals, but they offer a pretty good indication of what enthusiasts are shopping for. Here are nine of the most popular choices, and why people want them.

The Nissan Skyline GT-R is arguably Nissan's most famous performance car and the Skyline family commands an extraordinary share of enthusiast import attention. On the JDMBuySell top 10 ranking of what JDM buyers are watching, the Skyline holds not just the top spot, but three of the top four. The R34 leads the pack as number one, the R32 is number three, and the R33 takes fourth.

There's plenty of substance behind the Skyline's mythological status. When Nissan revived the GT-R with the R32 in 1989, it did so with a 2.6-liter twin-turbocharged inline-6 with electronically controlled four-wheel drive and four-wheel multilink suspension. The R33 and R34 followed, iterating on the formula, and eventually giving enthusiasts three generations of increasingly sophisticated performance machinery to choose from.

Yet one of the biggest reasons the GT-R holds a special place in so many enthusiasts' hearts is that Americans got a taste of the legend long before they could legally import one. It was a GT-R on the cover of the original Gran Turismo video game for PlayStation in 1997. Considering that the Gran Turismo franchise has sold more than 90 million copies globally, a whole lot of kids grew up experiencing the car digitally decades before they could even consider getting their hands on the real thing.

Back to that "add 25" math: As of 2024, each of these three generations had at the least begun qualifying for import, with later examples becoming eligible every year. Being allowed to buy one is one thing, though, and paying for one is quite another.

The history of Mazda's most famous rotary powered car is full of nuance and enthusiast nerdery. This specific case, the JDM-spec RX-7 FD, is a perfect example of that, holding sixth place in those JDMBuySell popularity rankings. But it's also the one car on this list where the unfamiliar might rightfully ask, "Wait a minute, couldn't you buy these in the United States?" The answer is ... sort of.

That's because American RX-7 sales ended after the 1995 model year, while the Japanese market continued having access to new examples all the way through 2002. That opens up the possibility not just of a half-decade-newer car, but one that reflects years of additional refinement and development. In fact, a major update in 1999 included a turbocharger upgrade, better cooling, and updates to the suspension, plus revisions to the aero that included a rad rear wing.

raw_title: What The Bird On The Pontiac Trans Am's Hood Is Actually Called
title: What The Bird On The Pontiac Trans Am's Hood Is Actually Called
raw_summary: It's been a century since Pontiac was founded, and while the brand was discontinued 16 years ago, the Firebird Trans Am still stands out as its most recognizable and iconic model — aside from the turbocharged Trans Am that is. Built over four generations and 35 years, the Firebird is a legendary pony car much like the Ford Mustang. One of its most unique elements was the optional bird graphic across the hood, often referred to as the 'screaming chicken.' The story of how this graphic came to be is fascinating. When the original Firebird launched in 1967, it sported an emblem of a bird with its wings down and beak closed, much like Hopi Native American jewelry. The famed phoenix graphic later featured on the Firebird Trans Am built on this emblem, with Pontiac head of design Bill Porter adding dramatic wings and gold feathers. These elements were inspired by colorful Tiffany vases that he collected.

Built over four generations and 35 years, the Firebird is a legendary pony car much like the Ford Mustang.
article_paragraphs: It's been a century since Pontiac was founded, and while the brand was discontinued 16 years ago, the Firebird Trans Am still stands out as its most recognizable and iconic model — aside from the turbocharged Trans Am that is. Built over four generations and 35 years, the Firebird is a legendary pony car much like the Ford Mustang. One of its most unique elements was the optional bird graphic across the hood, often referred to as the 'screaming chicken.' The story of how this graphic came to be is fascinating.

When the original Firebird launched in 1967, it sported an emblem of a bird with its wings down and beak closed, much like Hopi Native American jewelry. The famed phoenix graphic later featured on the Firebird Trans Am built on this emblem, with Pontiac head of design Bill Porter adding dramatic wings and gold feathers. These elements were inspired by colorful Tiffany vases that he collected.

Porter was so eager to see his design added to the Firebird that while the 1970 model was being developed, he printed and stuck the graphic onto a full-sized clay model. Speaking with Original MotorCar in 2024, Porter revealed that then-GM design boss Bill Mitchell spotted the graphic and hated it. At the time, it seemed like that might have been the end of the bird and with it, any chance of epic future restomodded Trans Ams.

It wasn't until a couple of years later that GM designer John Schinella discovered Porter's design, enhanced it, and re-pitched the idea to Mitchell. To give himself the best chance of having the design approved, he applied a gold graphic to the hood of a black Trans Am after noticing Mitchell owned a black motorcycle adorned with gold graphics. As fate would have it, his plan worked, and Mitchell approved it.

In addition to being called the 'screaming chicken,' the graphic is also referred to by some as a 'rising phoenix,' but was actually just called the Trans Am Hood Decal by Pontiac. It debuted as an option on the 1973 Firebird Trans Am, costing $55, and proved extremely popular. The bird was originally 45.5 inches wide and 44.5 inches long, and in 1978, it grew in size to 47 inches wide by 55 inches tall. The bird's head was also repositioned and no longer pointed toward the driver, but instead faced the passenger side.

This enlarged version of the graphic became standard on all 1979 Trans Am models, except the 10 th Anniversary version. The pattern then grew slightly for 1980 Trans Ams — which became an ideal Firebird restomod platform in 2022 — and spawned a unique version for the Firebird's turbocharged models. At the height of its popularity in the late 1970s, the design was such a hit that even Ford copied it, placing a large golden snake graphic on the Mustang King Cobra hood. The third-generation Firebird, introduced in 1982, continued to offer the distinctive graphic, though it was smaller than previous iterations. Ultimately, the graphic's popularity waned, and Pontiac dropped it for the 1988 model.

title: Why F1's 2026 cars are unusually quick in Mexico
raw_summary: A combination of factors means Formula 1's 2026 cars have been unusually close to the performance of their ground-effect predecessors in Mexico. Charles Leclerc's FP1-topping time, a 1m18.128s, was 0.252s quicker than the lap he set to lead first practice in Mexico last year. Charles Leclerc's FP1-topping time, a 1m18.128s, was 0.252s quicker than the lap he set to lead first practice in Mexico last year. That's the first time the 2026 cars have outpaced the 2025 cars in an FP1 session, having usually been two or three seconds slower.
Leclerc lowered the bar by three tenths to a 1m17.827s in FP2, though that was 0.435s slower than Max Verstappen's FP2 benchmark from last year.
Pirelli's pre-weekend simulations had predicted a 1m17.0s would be pole position, but after Friday's running it's now predicted to be well below that.
Pole position last year - a 1m15.586s - ended up being 1.8s faster than the pace in FP2, so you'd expect the 2026 pole position to be in the low-1m16s.
That should mean the smallest 2025 versus 2026 dry-weather qualifying difference of the season, with the previous closest being 1.409s in Baku.
So why are the 2026 cars so competitive at the Mexican Grand Prix relative to their ground-effect-era predecessors?
The track underwent a partial resurfacing ahead of the 2026 race, with resurfacing work taking place from Turn 10 to Turn 1.

raw_title: The Pros And Cons Of Getting Multiple Car Insurance Quotes
title: The Pros And Cons Of Getting Multiple Car Insurance Quotes
raw_summary: Shopping around for auto insurance probably sounds like as much fun as cleaning tile grout. With car insurance, it's much easier just to renew your old policy instead of comparing rates. At least with grout cleaning you'll have a clean bathroom afterward. But there are definite advantages to getting multiple car insurance quotes once a year or so. For one thing, statistics show there is a very real possibility you will save money if you compare rates from multiple companies, though you could be among the fortunate few who already have the lowest rate on the market. No doubt, that's a big part of the reason more customers are switching away from some of the biggest insurers than are switching to them. Shopping around also makes it easy to find coverage more suited for your current circumstances. You may also find that your current carrier has been regularly raising your rates a little whenever renewal time comes around just because it can. Researching other carriers can also help if you're not satisfied with the customer service or claims handling of your current insurer.

article_paragraphs: Shopping around for auto insurance probably sounds like as much fun as cleaning tile grout. With car insurance, it's much easier just to renew your old policy instead of comparing rates. At least with grout cleaning you'll have a clean bathroom afterward. But there are definite advantages to getting multiple car insurance quotes once a year or so.

For one thing, statistics show there is a very real possibility you will save money if you compare rates from multiple companies, though you could be among the fortunate few who already have the lowest rate on the market. No doubt, that's a big part of the reason more customers are switching away from some of the biggest insurers than are switching to them. Shopping around also makes it easy to find coverage more suited for your current circumstances. You may also find that your current carrier has been regularly raising your rates a little whenever renewal time comes around just because it can. Researching other carriers can also help if you're not satisfied with the customer service or claims handling of your current insurer.

Now, there can be cons to getting multiple insurance quotes, believe it or not. Contrary to popular belief, though, your credit taking a hit is not one of those cons. That's a myth. However, entering your contact information into several websites will get you a ton of spam calls and email. Shopping around can be time-consuming. And you may accidentally cause your insurance to lapse if you're not careful.

Let's be honest; money is the reason most of those who think about shopping around for car insurance would switch. And it's why so many drivers are reducing or dropping their insurance . This isn't that surprising in a time when we're paying over $4 a gallon for both gas and milk. According to a Consumer Reports survey, 58% of respondents who left their past provider said they did it because another company had better rates, while 41% switched because their old provider raised rates.
And the savings are real. Among those who switched, the median price decrease was $461 annually. In fact, 41% said they paid at least $500 less, and 13% said their cost dropped at least $1,000.

Consumer Reports recommends shopping around for better rates every year or two, and we would have to agree. Comparison is the only way to know if you're getting the best rates and might even help keep insurers stay competitive in their pricing. You could also find out about discounts you've haven't taken advantage of. Comparing rates is so important that the California Insurance Code requires the state to publish a comparison of insurance rates report every year. The California Department of Insurance says that "it is important to remember to shop for insurance in the same way that you shop for any other consumer product."

So you're on a comparison website searching for comprehensive insurance, and the page returns five insurance company names, each with its monthly or annual premium next to its name. Just choose the lowest one, right? Or maybe you call up one of your current insurer's competitors and they tell you they'll give you comprehensive coverage for $20 a month less than what you're paying now. Pretty cut- and-dried, right?

Not so fast. In cases like that, it's not just the premiums you should be looking at. For example, what are the deductibles? A deductible is the amount you have to pay first before an insurance company pays on a claim. Deductibles can range anywhere from $100 to $2,000. So, for instance, say you file a claim for $2,500 in damage, but your deductible is $2,000. You'll have to pay $2,000 toward fixing your car while the insurance company only pays $500. The bottom line: If a policy with a slightly lower premium has a much higher deductible, it may not be worth it to switch.

raw_summary: Sepang produced another chaotic MotoGP sprint, as Pedro Acosta walked away with the race victory and Marc Marquez established an ever-increasing grip on the riders’ title. After the 10-lap sprint in near-mixed conditions, here are our winners and losers.

article_paragraphs: Sepang produced another chaotic MotoGP sprint, as Pedro Acosta walked away with the race victory and Marc Marquez established an ever-increasing grip on the riders’ title.
After the 10-lap sprint in near-mixed conditions, here are our winners and losers.

Out of Acosta's three various-distance race wins in MotoGP so far, this one may well be the nicest - though he admitted it owed a lot to him having no championship implications to worry about unlike Marquez and Marco Bezzecchi.

Considering he isn't really convinced about his strengths in this kind of mixed weather, this was an important win, too, and certainly not something that would dissuade you if you have him pegged as a 2027 title favourite.
Marquez marches on, muffling the heartbeats of the already on-life-support title battle.

This was a slightly precarious race, though not quite as precarious as it could've been. It was just controllable enough for Marquez to control it exactly to his liking - as his gameplan was to stay ahead of Bezzecchi but also to not lead, to not be the pathfinder having to figure out the wet patches.

It worked out well, and while he should have been beaten by his brother today, he wasn't, meaning that it's now been 12 races (across GPs and sprints) since Marquez last wasn't the top Ducati in the classification.

It’s not too far-fetched to say the younger Marquez was a pre-weekend contender for a potential 37-point haul, and he looked well on-course when he took pole position and built up a healthy lead three laps into the sprint.

raw_title: Why I Converted My 1979 Volvo 245 From Fuel Injection To Carburetion
title: Why I Converted My 1979 Volvo 245 From Fuel Injection To Carburetion
raw_summary: That's my brick. It's a faded red. Officially, Volvo calls it Cimarron Red, but why didn't they just call it Brick? Anyway, the hue isn't — or at least hasn't been — my focus since I acquired the car from Eureka, California, a year and a half ago. Yes, I also hunted Volvo 145s, but most I spied needed way too much TLC — like this one . There was just one problem with my brick: The prior owner ditched the stock fuel injection, known as Bosch K-Jetronic, which came on U.S.- and Canadian-bound versions of the B21F engine in the late 1970s. Instead, he switched to a throttle-body fuel injection , by way of the Holley Sniper EFI 1100. The car never ran right with the Holley, and my mechanic friend, Ryan, made two damning points about its shortcomings. First, it lacks an Internal Air Temperature sensor (IAT). For about the same $1,100, Summit Racing sells a throttle body kit with an IAT, but it didn't come on the Holley. Ryan said the reason that matters is because you want a live reading of air density during combustion. He explained that Holley's downstream sensing (in the exhaust) was always back-calibrating the ratio of fuel and air. The system I had also only allowed code tweaks via an SD card.

article_paragraphs: That's my brick. It's a faded red. Officially, Volvo calls it Cimarron Red, but why didn't they just call it Brick? Anyway, the hue isn't — or at least hasn't been — my focus since I acquired the car from Eureka, California, a year and a half ago. Yes, I also hunted Volvo 145s, but most I spied needed way too much TLC — like this one . There was just one problem with my brick: The prior owner ditched the stock fuel injection, known as Bosch K-Jetronic, which came on U.S.- and Canadian-bound versions of the B21F engine in the late 1970s. Instead, he switched to a throttle-body fuel injection , by way of the Holley Sniper EFI 1100. The car never ran right with the Holley, and my mechanic friend, Ryan, made two damning points about its shortcomings.

First, it lacks an Internal Air Temperature sensor (IAT). For about the same $1,100, Summit Racing sells a throttle body kit with an IAT, but it didn't come on the Holley. Ryan said the reason that matters is because you want a live reading of air density during combustion. He explained that Holley's downstream sensing (in the exhaust) was always back-calibrating the ratio of fuel and air. The system I had also only allowed code tweaks via an SD card.

Sure, you could purchase a setup to live-calibrate the Holley with a laptop, but without an IAT, I would still have zero guarantee of smooth operation in the future. So, I was left with two choices: to find a salvaged K-Jetronic, or go even farther back in time and revert to a carburetor. I went the latter route, and the decision came down to me being a cheap automotive journalist. Well, mostly.

Trust me, I considered finding a viable K-Jetronic mechanical fuel-injection solution. K-Jet in various forms dates all the way to the late 1960s, and was used by many other carmakers, including Volkswagen and Mercedes-Benz. I'm not telling you exactly what I paid for my car, but I will tell you, as I already have, that it wasn't a fortune — nor do I have one to spend on making a not-mint Volvo into a parts-perfect museum piece.

Just to make this clear, K-Jet consists of a fuel pump, accumulator, fuel filter, airflow sensor, warm-up regulator, fuel distributor, injectors, cold start injector, Thermotime switch, and auxiliary air device. I'd need to acquire all of that. Then I'd need the right manifold, too, since that was long gone from my car. I'd also have to fetch the correct wiring harness for $320 from an outfit called, fittingly, Prancing Moose. I'd already sourced a harness from there for the overdrive my buddy Joe put in my car. I held the flashlights and whinged along with Joe, who did all the actual work and troubleshooting.

Anyway, even tabulating costs with a dull pencil and a greasy napkin, I was sure going the K-Jet path would cost me far north of $1,000. Yep, a junkyard K-Jet might work. Or I might be rebuilding every single part. Rebuild kits exist from the likes of Volvo parts supplier IPD and Australia's K-Jet Specialists . Still, assembly would be delicate and fussy, and I'd need tools I don't have, like pressure-testing equipment required to get the calibration just right.

Going the carb route wasn't as crazy as it sounds. My same 240, sold in other markets, got a B21A engine with a Stromberg carburetor. And, actually, the last carbureted car sold new in America was on the market in 1994, which just shows you that early fuel injection hardly convinced every carmaker that it was the perfect fueling solution. As for which carb path to take, I could have spent $892.14 for that original B21A Stromberg. But why do that when Classic Car Performance sells a complete Weber 32/36 DGEV conversion kit for $569.99? And because the Holley conversion meant I already had a perfectly good Pierce manifold on the 245, I knocked off another hundred bucks by not needing that part.

As I saw it, the benefit of deciding to use the Weber was relatively simple tuning and mechanical simplicity. As a reminder, a carburetor has jets that are essentially screws with holes in them precisely sized to allow the right amount of fuel to get sucked in as air passes through the barrel (or barrels), controlled by a drop in pressure, and the gas-and-air mixture gets ignited within the engine.

title: Inside Herta's Cadillac F1 audition
raw_summary: Colton Herta might still somehow be one superlicence point short of a Formula 1 superlicence after a bizarre error, but his latest Cadillac F1 outing was an important audition to replace Valtteri Bottas next year. An incorrect calculation of his superlicence points (verified at the time by the FIA) means Herta erroneously thought completing 30 laps in his fifth FP1 outing of the season in Mexico would be enough to take him to the 40-point threshold required to finally earn him the superlicence he’s been chasing for years.
summary: Colton Herta might still somehow be one superlicence point short of a Formula 1 superlicence after a bizarre error, but his latest Cadillac F1 outing was an important audition to replace Valtteri Bottas next year.
article_paragraphs: Colton Herta might still somehow be one superlicence point short of a Formula 1 superlicence after a bizarre error, but his latest Cadillac F1 outing was an important audition to replace Valtteri Bottas next year.

An incorrect calculation of his superlicence points (verified at the time by the FIA) means Herta erroneously thought completing 30 laps in his fifth FP1 outing of the season in Mexico would be enough to take him to the 40-point threshold required to finally earn him the superlicence he’s been chasing for years.
“I was literally walking to go do the media stuff [after FP2], that was like the first time I had heard about it,” Herta said on Friday evening.
“Obviously, we were still doing our meetings and whatnot, so I haven't talked to anybody about it. As far as I was concerned, going into the weekend, if I did 100km here, I would have 40 [points].

“So, I'm not sure what's changed, or why stuff has changed, or if it even has. I have to wait and see. I think a lot of the people that I want to talk to about this are still in the meeting. Maybe I'll have a little bit more clarity this evening.”

Cadillac has gone beyond the mandated four rookie practice outings and given Herta a fifth session in Mexico to get him an extra point. Cadillac will run him again to get the final point, and had planned to anyway before the bizarre calculation error emerged.

But his Mexico outing wasn’t a case of Herta simply cruising around to get the mandated 100km of running to get the point. He was given an extensive programme that wasn’t too dissimilar from Perez's, his 2027 team-mate, should he secure Bottas’s race seat.
Herta’s FP1 starts with an 11-lap stint on the hard tyres with a best lap of 1m22.452s, 1.067s slower than Perez’s on the same tyres.

raw_title: Acosta wins chaotic Sepang MotoGP sprint
title: Acosta wins chaotic Sepang MotoGP sprint
raw_summary: Pedro Acosta claimed victory in a bizarre Sepang MotoGP sprint that was threatened by rain late on. Acosta came out on top of a four-way battle for the race win, prevailing by 0.578s over Marc Marquez, who increased his championship chances with second place.
summary: Pedro Acosta claimed victory in a bizarre Sepang MotoGP sprint that was threatened by rain late on. Acosta came out on top of a four-way battle for the race win, prevailing by 0.578s over Marc Marquez, who increased his championship chances with second place.
article_paragraphs: Pedro Acosta claimed victory in a bizarre Sepang MotoGP sprint that was threatened by rain late on.
Acosta came out on top of a four-way battle for the race win, prevailing by 0.578s over Marc Marquez, who increased his championship chances with second place.
Marquez is now 19 points up on the absent Jorge Martin, and 52 points clear of Marco Bezzecchi.
His brother Alex Marquez had got the start from pole position and led uncontested for four laps until he slid out of the race lead at Turn 14.
The lead was then inherited by Ai Ogura, who had moved up to second place after an aggressive opening corner tussle with Marc.

Spots of rain meant the white flag came out on lap two, allowing riders to swap bikes - with Jack Miller immediately prepared to take the gamble, but his Pramac Yamaha team not ready with his second bike, which frustrated him to no end.

Iker Lecuona, Joan Mir and Franco Morbidelli were the first group to come in and successfully switch on lap five, but were setting times almost 10 seconds off the leaders’ pace, with Maverick Vinales the only other rider electing to change towards the end of the race.
In the tricky conditions the top four bunched up, Ogura managing to hold off the challenges until Acosta attacked with three laps to spare.

title: Martin admits MotoGP title 'already lost' after Sepang withdrawal
raw_summary: Aprilia MotoGP rider Jorge Martin feels the 2026 title is "already lost" following his withdrawal from the Malaysian Grand Prix weekend - but intends to ride in Qatar next week. Martin sustained a distal radius fracture in a crash during the Phillip Island sprint, but was back to riding just six days later at Sepang, in a desperate bid to keep himself in the championship picture and minimise the damage versus points leader Marc Marquez.
summary: Aprilia MotoGP rider Jorge Martin feels the 2026 title is "already lost" following his withdrawal from the Malaysian Grand Prix weekend - but intends to ride in Qatar next week. Martin sustained a distal radius fracture in a crash during the Phillip Island sprint, but was back to riding just six days later at Sepang, in a desperate bid to keep himself in the championship picture and minimise the damage versus points leader Marc Marquez.
article_paragraphs: Aprilia MotoGP rider Jorge Martin feels the 2026 title is "already lost" following his withdrawal from the Malaysian Grand Prix weekend - but intends to ride in Qatar next week.

Martin sustained a distal radius fracture in a crash during the Phillip Island sprint, but was back to riding just six days later at Sepang, in a desperate bid to keep himself in the championship picture and minimise the damage versus points leader Marc Marquez.
But Martin was forced to give up on his weekend after three sessions, withdrawing after Saturday morning practice.
"I tried, I tried my best, I tried to ride, but for sure the process of healing is still early," he explained afterwards.

"The healing is going really fast, but not enough to be efficient on the bike. I felt that I could ride with almost no pain, but for maybe one lap. After that I started to have a lot of pain, I couldn't be constant, so watching a bit the laptimes and my performance, we decided to stop, to try to wait.
"We thought together with the team that the effort I was doing was too much to continue and yeah, nothing to gain. It was just going to be very difficult even to score one point."

Martin said he just didn't have the requisite strength under braking - and made reference to his past efforts to shortcut recovery periods, particularly in an injury-laden 2025 and specifically in his return to racing in Qatar last year, in which he ran out of energy in the race, crashed and suffered a bad injury after being hit by a rival bike.
"It wasn't the best idea to continue," he said of this weekend, "because if I continue, it [shows] that I haven't learned anything from the past.

title: Martin out of Sepang MotoGP weekend, Alex Marquez on pole
raw_summary: Alex Marquez took pole position for MotoGP's Malaysian Grand Prix and the sprint, as title hopeful Jorge Martin withdrew from the Sepang weekend. Martin, who fractured his wrist a week ago at Phillip Island, did three runs totalling eight laps in the 30-minute practice session before qualifying, and had to concede defeat in terms of continuing with the weekend.
summary: Alex Marquez took pole position for MotoGP's Malaysian Grand Prix and the sprint, as title hopeful Jorge Martin withdrew from the Sepang weekend. Martin, who fractured his wrist a week ago at Phillip Island, did three runs totalling eight laps in the 30-minute practice session before qualifying, and had to concede defeat in terms of continuing with the weekend.
article_paragraphs: Alex Marquez took pole position for MotoGP's Malaysian Grand Prix and the sprint, as title hopeful Jorge Martin withdrew from the Sepang weekend.

Martin, who fractured his wrist a week ago at Phillip Island, did three runs totalling eight laps in the 30-minute practice session before qualifying, and had to concede defeat in terms of continuing with the weekend.
"His feeling was better, to be honest, compared with yesterday, but he was not able to force in the braking," Aprilia team manager Paolo Bonora told MotoGP.com.

"The plan is to come back to Spain as soon as possible and to push on the recovery and to do his best to recover the situation. Coming back to Spain immediately, and then we check all together, during all the days, the situation, how it is improving, and we focus to have him in Qatar."
With Martin now consigned to a non-score at Sepang, points leader Marc Marquez was close to maximising his qualifying, ultimately just 0.070s short of beating his brother.
Alex Marquez had been the leader after the initial Q2 runs already, but was shuffled down to fifth by the end of the session - only to respond with a 1m56.493s that snatched pole from Marc.
Pedro Acosta on the KTM will join the pair on the front row, having followed the elder Marquez very closely on both Q2 runs.
Aprilia pair Ai Ogura and Marco Bezzecchi completed a top five covered by just 0.175s, with Fabio Di Giannantonio in sixth another 0.174s back from Bezzecchi.
